questions.question: Do you work or are you a student?
questions.answer: I'm a full-time student at the moment — I'm in my third year of an economics degree. I actually took a gap year before university, so I'm slightly older than most of my classmates. Alongside my studies, I do a bit of freelance translation on the side, which helps me cover my expenses.

vocab.meaning: spend a year not studying, usually before university
vocab.uz: o'qishdan oldin bir yillik tanaffus qilmoq

vocab.meaning: at the same time as studying
in addition to your main job or study
pay for the things I need

questions.question: What do you like about your studies / work?
questions.answer: What I enjoy most is that the subject is intellectually stimulating — I'm constantly coming across ideas that make me rethink things. I also like the fact that it's very hands-on; we work on real case studies rather than just memorising theory. And honestly, the people on my course are brilliant, so the whole thing feels collaborative rather than competitive.

vocab.meaning: makes you think in an interesting way
meet or find something by chance
practical, involving doing rather than watching
learn theory by heart without understanding
based on working together, not on beating others

questions.question: Is there anything you dislike about it?
questions.answer: If I'm honest, the workload can be relentless, especially around exam season. There are weeks when I'm juggling four deadlines at once and I barely have time to breathe. I also find some of the lectures a bit dry — they could be far more engaging if they cut down on the slides and let us discuss things instead.

vocab.meaning: is relentless the amount of work never lets up
manage several demanding things at once
vocab.uz: bir vaqtning o'zida bir nechta ishni eplab ketmoq

vocab.meaning: boring, with no life in it (of a lesson or book) zerikarli, quruq cut down on reduce the amount of something

questions.question: Would you like to change your major / job in the future?
questions.answer: I don't think I'd switch completely, but I could see myself branching out into something more data-driven, like analytics. Economics gives you a solid foundation, so it's fairly easy to pivot later on. That said, I'm trying not to map everything out too rigidly — I'd rather keep my options open and see where things take me.

vocab.meaning: move into a new area or field
not commit to one choice yet

practice.question: Why did you choose your subject or your job?
practice.answer: Honestly, it was a gradual decision. I took a gap year after school and did some bookkeeping on the side for a relative, which turned out to be surprisingly hands-on. That's when I realised economics wasn't just abstract theory, so I applied the following spring.

practice.question: How do you balance your studies or work with the rest of your life?
practice.answer: Not always successfully! The workload is relentless in the last weeks of each term, and I end up juggling deadlines with my translation work. Still, the translating covers my expenses, so I can't really drop it. I try to keep Sundays completely free, which helps.

practice.question: What would your ideal job be?
practice.answer: Something international — ideally at a development bank. That said, I'd like to branch out into data analysis at some point, so I'm keeping my options open rather than committing to one path too early.

questions.question: Where is your hometown?
questions.answer: I'm originally from Namangan, which is tucked away in the Fergana Valley in the east of Uzbekistan. It's about a five-hour drive from the capital, or a short flight if you're in a rush. I moved to Tashkent for university, but I still go back every couple of months to see family.

vocab.meaning: located in a quiet or hidden place

questions.question: What's your hometown well-known for?
questions.answer: It's probably best known for its craftsmanship — pottery and silk in particular have been made there for centuries. The city also has a bit of a reputation for flowers; there's an enormous rose garden that people travel from all over the country to see. And of course, like anywhere in the valley, the food is second to none.

vocab.meaning: skill in making things by hand

vocab.uz: biror narsa bilan nom chiqargan bo'lmoq

questions.question: Is it a good place to raise kids?
questions.answer: I'd say it's ideal, actually. It's safe enough that children can play outside without their parents worrying, which is becoming rare these days. There's also a very strong sense of community — neighbours genuinely look out for one another. The one drawback is that opportunities are limited once kids grow up, so a lot of families end up moving to the capital.

vocab.meaning: so safe that something is possible
the feeling that people belong together

questions.question: Is there anything you dislike about your hometown?
questions.answer: The traffic has got noticeably worse over the last few years — the roads simply weren't built to cope with that many cars. I'd also say the city shuts down quite early; if you fancy going out after ten, your options are pretty thin on the ground. But those are minor gripes, really.

practice.question: Do you still live in your hometown?
practice.answer: No, I moved to Tashkent for university, but I go back most holidays. My family's house is tucked away in a quiet street near the old bazaar, so every visit feels like stepping into a slower version of my life.

practice.question: What do visitors usually do in your hometown?
practice.answer: Most of them head straight for the workshops. The city has a reputation for pottery and silk, and the craftsmanship is honestly second to none — some families have made the same patterns for generations. Decent hotels are still thin on the ground, though.

practice.question: How has your hometown changed in recent years?
practice.answer: It's grown a lot. There are new apartment blocks on the outskirts, but the roads simply weren't built to cope with so many cars. That's a minor gripe, though — what matters more is that a sense of community hasn't disappeared.

part1.name: House and Apartment

questions.question: Do you live in a house or an apartment?
questions.answer: I live in a flat — it's on the sixth floor of a fairly typical block. It's compact, but it's been done up nicely and it gets a lot of natural light, which makes it feel bigger than it is. I'd love a house with a garden one day, but for now a flat suits my lifestyle perfectly.

vocab.meaning: small but well organised ixcham, kichik lekin qulay do (a place) up renovate or decorate it

vocab.phrase: get a lot of natural light

vocab.meaning: at some point in the future

questions.question: What can you see from the windows of your home?
questions.answer: From the living room I've got a fairly unremarkable view of the car park and the building opposite. But the bedroom window looks out over a small park, so in spring I can see the trees coming into bloom. On a clear day you can just about make out the mountains in the distance, which is my favourite part.

questions.question: What colour would you choose to paint your room?
questions.answer: I'd go for something muted — probably a soft sage green or a warm off-white. Those shades are easy on the eye and they make a room feel calm rather than cluttered. I might then add colour through cushions and artwork, so I can change the mood without repainting the whole thing.

vocab.meaning: full of too many things, messy

questions.question: Is there any colour you would never use for your room?
questions.answer: Bright red, without a doubt. I find it far too overpowering for a space where you're meant to relax — it almost puts you on edge. Black would be another one; it might look sophisticated in photos, but in reality it would swallow all the light and make the room feel like a cave.

vocab.meaning: absorb the light and make a place dark

questions.question: Which room does your family spend most of the time in?
questions.answer: Definitely the kitchen — it's the heart of the home in our family. Even though we've got a perfectly good living room, everyone gravitates towards the kitchen table. That's where we eat, argue, do homework and catch up on each other's news, usually all at the same time.

vocab.meaning: find out what has happened recently

practice.question: What's your favourite room in your home?
practice.answer: It has to be the living room. It gets a lot of natural light in the afternoon and looks out over a small garden, so it's where I read. It's also the heart of the home — everyone ends up there in the evening to catch up on each other's news.

practice.question: Is there anything you would like to change about your home?
practice.answer: I'd love to do up the kitchen at some point. It's quite compact, and because there's so little storage, the worktops always look cluttered. With better shelves and lighter tiles, it would feel twice the size.

practice.question: Do you prefer modern or traditional decoration?
practice.answer: Modern, but not the cold, minimalist kind. I like simple furniture and soft, neutral colours that are easy on the eye, mixed with one or two traditional pieces — a handwoven rug, for instance — so the place still has some character.

phraseBank: get a lot of natural light

questions.question: Can you describe the area where you live?
questions.answer: It's a residential neighbourhood about twenty minutes from the centre — leafy, quiet, and mostly families rather than students. Everything you need is within walking distance: a couple of supermarkets, a pharmacy, a decent bakery. It's not the most exciting part of town, but it's incredibly convenient and I've never once felt unsafe there.

vocab.meaning: an area of housing, not shops or offices

questions.question: How long have you lived there?
questions.answer: I've been living there for about six years now. We moved in when I started secondary school, so I've more or less grown up in that neighbourhood. It's strange — when we first arrived it felt completely unfamiliar, and now I could walk home from anywhere with my eyes closed.

vocab.meaning: start living in a new place

questions.question: Do you think you'll continue living there in the future?
questions.answer: Probably not indefinitely, no. I'd like to live abroad for a few years to broaden my horizons, and realistically my career will dictate where I end up. Having said that, I can absolutely imagine settling down there later in life — it's the kind of place that's much better for raising a family than for being twenty-two.

vocab.meaning: start a stable, permanent life somewhere

questions.question: What do you like most about your area?
questions.answer: The pace of life, I think. It's noticeably slower than the city centre — you can actually hear birds in the morning instead of car horns. I also really appreciate that the neighbours keep an eye on each other's houses. That kind of quiet solidarity is something you don't get in a big anonymous apartment block.

vocab.meaning: how fast or slow daily life is

questions.question: Is there anything you'd love to change about it?
questions.answer: I'd love to see more green space — there's one small playground and that's about it. A proper park would make a world of difference, especially for the older residents. The other thing is public transport; the bus service is patchy in the evenings, so you're more or less reliant on taxis after dark.

vocab.meaning: parks and open natural areas in a city
inconsistent, good in parts and bad in others beqaror, uzuq-yuluq be reliant on depend on

practice.question: What do people in your area usually do in the evenings?
practice.answer: It's mostly a residential neighbourhood, so evenings are fairly calm. Families stroll along the leafy streets, older neighbours sit outside and keep an eye on the kids playing, and teenagers gather at the one small café we have.

practice.question: Is it easy to get around your area?
practice.answer: On foot, yes — most shops and the clinic are within walking distance. Getting to the city centre is harder, though. The buses are infrequent, so most people are reliant on taxis or their own cars.

practice.question: Would you recommend your area to a friend?
practice.answer: Definitely, if they value peace and quiet. The pace of life is slower than in the centre, and there's plenty of green space, which makes a world of difference when you've spent all day staring at a screen.

questions.question: Do you usually recycle your rubbish?
questions.answer: I try to, though I'll admit I'm not as diligent as I should be. I always separate plastic bottles and paper because there are dedicated bins near my building. Glass is trickier — the nearest collection point is a bus ride away, so it tends to fall by the wayside. It's something I'd like to get better at.

vocab.meaning: careful and consistent in doing something
a bin for one specific type of waste

questions.question: What kind of rubbish do you usually throw away?
questions.answer: Mostly food waste and packaging, unfortunately — almost everything you buy these days comes wrapped in three layers of plastic. I also get through a fair amount of paper because of university printouts. What I try hard to avoid is single-use items like coffee cups; I carry a reusable one instead.

vocab.meaning: (an amount) use up a quantity of something
designed to be used once and thrown away

questions.question: How often do you throw away rubbish?
questions.answer: I take the bin out every other day, roughly. In summer it has to be daily, otherwise the kitchen starts to smell within hours. The building has a communal chute, so it's genuinely no effort — I think if it were harder, I'd be far more conscious of how much I actually produce.

vocab.meaning: once every two days kun ora within hours in a very short time

questions.question: Is there a lot of rubbish in the area where you live?
questions.answer: Not really, no — the streets are kept remarkably clean. The council sends street sweepers round early every morning, and most people are fairly civic-minded about not dropping litter. You do occasionally see rubbish piling up near the containers on collection day, but it's cleared quickly enough.

vocab.meaning: caring about your community and public spaces

questions.question: What do you do when you see rubbish on the street?
questions.answer: If it's right in front of me and there's a bin nearby, I'll pick it up — it takes two seconds. I won't pretend I do it every single time, though. What I definitely won't do is turn a blind eye if I see someone littering deliberately; I'd probably say something, politely. I think that kind of social pressure is more effective than fines.

vocab.meaning: influence from the people around you

practice.question: Do people produce more rubbish now than in the past?
practice.answer: Without a doubt. My grandparents barely threw anything away, whereas now almost everything comes in single-use packaging. We take the bin out every other day, and most of it is plastic wrappers rather than food waste.

practice.question: Did your school teach you about recycling?
practice.answer: We had a recycling week once a year, and everyone was very diligent for those few days. Unfortunately, the habit fell by the wayside as soon as the posters came down, because there were no separate bins for the rest of the year.

practice.question: How could your city reduce the amount of rubbish on its streets?
practice.answer: Firstly, by fining people who drop litter — at the moment most officials turn a blind eye. More frequent collections would also help in busy areas, where bags tend to pile up by the kerb over the weekend.

questions.question: Do you like collecting things?
questions.answer: I went through a phase of it as a child — I collected fridge magnets from every city my family visited. These days I'm much less of a hoarder; I prefer to travel light and keep my space clear. The one thing I still hold on to is books, though I'm not sure that counts as collecting so much as simply refusing to throw them out.

vocab.meaning: do something for a limited period
vocab.uz: bir davrni boshdan kechirmoq, qiziqib yurmoq

vocab.meaning: someone who keeps far too many things

questions.question: What kinds of things are considered collectibles in your country?
questions.answer: Handicrafts are probably the biggest one — ceramics, embroidered fabrics, that sort of thing. Old coins and banknotes have quite a dedicated following too, especially Soviet-era ones. And among younger people, sneakers have become surprisingly collectible; some limited editions change hands for extraordinary sums.

questions.question: Is collecting a popular pastime in your country?
questions.answer: It's fairly niche, I'd say. Older generations tend to collect out of sentimental value rather than investment — stamps, photographs, letters. Younger people are more likely to collect digitally now, whether that's music or in-game items. So the underlying instinct hasn't gone away; it's just taken a different form.

vocab.meaning: appealing to a small, specific group
the basic natural urge behind something

questions.question: What are the benefits of collecting things?
questions.answer: I think the main one is that it teaches patience and persistence — you can't complete a collection overnight. It also gives people a shared interest, which is a brilliant way to meet others. And in some cases there's a genuine financial upside, though I'd argue that chasing the value rather defeats the point of the hobby.

vocab.meaning: the ability to wait and keep trying
a hobby people have in common
focus only on how much something is worth

practice.question: Did you collect anything as a child?
practice.answer: Yes, I went through a phase of collecting football stickers when I was about nine. Finishing the album took real patience and persistence — I spent months swapping duplicates at school, which was probably the best part.

practice.question: Do you keep things you don't really need?
practice.answer: Probably more than I should. I wouldn't call myself a hoarder, but I hold on to old letters and ticket stubs because they have sentimental value. Throwing them away would feel like throwing away the memories.

practice.question: Would you like to start a collection in the future?
practice.answer: Possibly. I've always admired local handicrafts, especially embroidered suzani, so I might collect small pieces. It's quite a niche hobby, but a friend of mine does it, so it would be a shared interest between us.

questions.question: Are you an ambitious person?
questions.answer: I'd say I am, though not in a cut-throat way. I'm the sort of person who sets themselves targets and quietly works towards them rather than announcing them to everyone. I think there's a difference between being ambitious and being driven by status — I'm much more motivated by getting good at something than by titles.

questions.question: Do you usually stick to your ambitions once you set them?
questions.answer: For the most part, yes — I'm quite stubborn once I've committed to something. Where I struggle is with goals that don't have a clear deadline; those tend to drift. So I've learned to break big ambitions into smaller monthly steps, which makes it far harder to let things slide.

vocab.meaning: continue with it, not give up
allow standards or effort to drop

questions.question: What was your ambition as a child?
questions.answer: I was absolutely set on becoming a pilot — I used to spend hours drawing aeroplanes and I would pester my parents to take me to the airport just to watch them take off. Looking back, I think what appealed to me wasn't flying itself so much as the idea of seeing the world. That part, at least, has stayed with me.

vocab.meaning: something be determined to do it
remain part of who I am

questions.question: How have your ambitions changed over time?
questions.answer: They've become far more grounded, I think. As a teenager I wanted the glamorous version of success — the job title, the city, the whole picture. Now I care much more about work-life balance and doing something that actually matters. I suppose that's just what happens as you come to terms with your own priorities.

vocab.meaning: attractive and exciting in a superficial way
a healthy split between job and personal life

practice.question: Is it important for young people to be ambitious?
practice.answer: I think so, as long as they stay grounded. Ambition gives you direction, and learning to set yourself targets early is a useful habit. The problem is when young people chase something glamorous they've only seen on social media.

practice.question: What is your biggest ambition right now?
practice.answer: At the moment I'm set on getting a band 8 in IELTS so I can apply for a master's abroad. I've made a study plan, and the real challenge is sticking to it on days when I'm tired and tempted to let things slide.

practice.question: Do your parents have ambitions for you?
practice.answer: Very much so! They'd love me to become a doctor, which isn't what I want. They've slowly come to terms with it, though, and these days they care more about me having a decent work-life balance than a prestigious title.

part1.name: Mirrors

questions.question: How often do you look at yourself in the mirror?
questions.answer: More than I'd like to admit, honestly. I check it properly twice a day — once when I'm getting ready in the morning and once before I leave the house in the evening. Beyond that it's mostly a quick glance to make sure my hair isn't all over the place. I wouldn't say I'm vain, just mildly self-conscious.

vocab.meaning: worried about how you appear to others

questions.question: Do you usually carry a mirror with you?
questions.answer: Not a proper one, no — I'd never think to put one in my bag. Like most people my age I just use my front-facing camera if I need to check something, which does the job perfectly well. My mother, on the other hand, has carried a small compact mirror for as long as I can remember; it's very much a generational thing.

vocab.meaning: the selfie camera on a phone old kamera (selfi kamerasi) do the job be good enough for the purpose

vocab.phrase: for as long as I can remember

vocab.meaning: a habit typical of one age group

questions.question: What are the main functions of a mirror?
questions.answer: The obvious one is practical — checking your appearance before you go out. But mirrors also play a big role in interior design; a well-placed one can make a small room feel twice the size because it bounces light around. And then there are specialised uses, like wing mirrors in cars, which are genuinely a matter of safety.

vocab.meaning: useful in a real, everyday way
the art of decorating indoor spaces ichki dizayn bounce light around reflect light through a space
an issue of protection from danger

questions.question: Would you use mirrors to decorate your room?
questions.answer: Absolutely — I think they're one of the most underrated decorating tools. My room doesn't get much afternoon sun, so a large mirror on the opposite wall would open the space up enormously. I'd go for one with an interesting frame, so it works as a feature in its own right rather than just a functional object.

vocab.meaning: not appreciated as much as it deserves
make a room feel larger and brighter

vocab.phrase: a feature in its own right

practice.question: Do you have many mirrors in your home?
practice.answer: Just a few. There's one in the hallway for a quick glance before I leave, and a bigger one in the bedroom where I get ready in the morning. My mum also hung one in the living room to bounce light around, because it's quite a dark room.

practice.question: Have you ever bought a mirror?
practice.answer: Yes, last year for my flat. I chose a tall one with a wooden frame, and it genuinely opened the space up — the room looks almost twice as big. It's become a feature in its own right rather than just something practical.

practice.question: Do people today spend too much time looking at themselves?
practice.answer: Probably, although it's more about phones than mirrors now. With a front-facing camera always in your pocket, it's easy to become self-conscious. Personally, I think a two-second look before going out does the job.

phraseBank: a feature in its own right

questions.question: Do you like listening to music?
questions.answer: I do — it's more or less the soundtrack to my day. I've got something playing from the moment I wake up until I go to bed, whether that's while I'm commuting, cooking or studying. I find it genuinely affects my mood; the right album can turn a bad morning around completely.

vocab.meaning: music playing constantly through the day
change it from bad to good

questions.question: What genres of music do you usually listen to?
questions.answer: My taste is fairly eclectic, but I gravitate towards indie rock and jazz. When I'm working I need something without lyrics, so I'll put on instrumental or lo-fi, otherwise I get distracted. And I've got a bit of a guilty pleasure for old Uzbek pop — it takes me straight back to childhood.

vocab.meaning: made up of many different styles rang-barang, turli uslublardan iborat gravitate towards be naturally drawn to
something you enjoy but feel slightly embarrassed about

questions.question: Have your music tastes changed over time?
questions.answer: Dramatically, yes. As a teenager I listened almost exclusively to whatever was in the charts — I was very much influenced by my friends. Over the last few years I've branched out a lot, partly thanks to streaming algorithms throwing things at me I'd never have found otherwise. My taste is far broader now, and much more genuinely my own.

vocab.meaning: be among the most popular songs
be affected in your choices by

questions.question: Can you play any musical instruments?
questions.answer: I dabbled in the guitar for a couple of years at school, but I never got beyond the basic chords. I can just about strum my way through a few songs if nobody's listening too closely. I regret giving it up, actually — it's one of those skills I'd love to pick back up when I've got more time.

vocab.meaning: try something without becoming serious about it
play a guitar by sweeping the strings
start doing it again after a break

practice.question: When do you usually listen to music?
practice.answer: Pretty much all the time — it's the soundtrack to my day. I put on something calm while I study and something much louder at the gym. I've noticed it really affects my mood, so I choose it quite carefully.

practice.question: Do you like the same music as your friends?
practice.answer: Not really. My friends mainly listen to Uzbek pop, whereas my taste is more eclectic. I tend to gravitate towards jazz and old soul, although I'll admit a few cheesy pop songs are a guilty pleasure of mine.

practice.question: Would you like to learn a musical instrument?
practice.answer: I'd love to. I dabbled in the dutar as a teenager but gave it up when exams took over. If I had more time, I'd definitely pick it back up, because I still remember the basics.

questions.question: Are you a tidy person?
questions.answer: I'd describe myself as selectively tidy. My desk and my kitchen are always spotless because I can't think clearly in a mess. My wardrobe, on the other hand, is a complete disaster — but since nobody sees it, I've made my peace with that. So I'm tidy where it counts, if that makes sense.

vocab.meaning: perfectly clean toza, bejirim a complete disaster extremely messy butunlay ostin-ustun make my peace with accept something I can't change

questions.question: How important is tidiness to you?
questions.answer: It matters more than I used to think. There's a real link between your surroundings and your state of mind — when my room is in chaos, I find it genuinely harder to concentrate. That said, I don't think it's worth becoming obsessive about; a home should look lived in, not like a show flat.

vocab.meaning: mental and emotional condition ruhiy holat in chaos in complete disorder

questions.question: Did your parents teach you to be tidy when you were a child?
questions.answer: They certainly tried. My mother was a stickler for making the bed every morning, and we weren't allowed to leave the table until everything was cleared away. At the time I found it tedious, but those habits stuck — I still can't leave the house with dishes in the sink.

vocab.meaning: someone who insists strictly on something
vocab.uz: biror narsani qat'iy talab qiladigan odam

vocab.meaning: tidy things and put them back

questions.question: Do you think being tidy is a habit or a personality trait?
questions.answer: I'd say it's a bit of both, but if I had to choose, I'd lean towards habit. Some people are naturally more orderly, of course, but tidiness is fundamentally something you train yourself into through repetition. I've seen naturally chaotic friends become very organised once they had their own place — which suggests it's learned rather than hard-wired.

vocab.meaning: partly one and partly the other ikkalasidan ham bor lean towards slightly prefer one option
naturally organised tartibli, uyushqoq train yourself into something develop it through practice
built into your nature from birth

practice.question: Is your desk usually tidy?
practice.answer: It depends on the week. I'm selectively tidy — my desk is spotless at the start of a project, but by the deadline it's usually a complete disaster, covered in coffee cups and printouts.

practice.question: Do you prefer living with tidy people?
practice.answer: Definitely, but not with someone who's a stickler for order. I once shared a room with a cousin who reorganised my books every day, which drove me mad. I lean towards people who are relaxed but still clear away their own mess.

practice.question: Which household chores do you dislike?
practice.answer: Ironing, without question. It's tedious, and I never seem to get it right. My sister actually enjoys it — I sometimes think her love of neatness is simply hard-wired.

questions.question: What kinds of websites do you often visit?
questions.answer: Mostly news sites and a couple of forums where people discuss things I'm interested in. I also spend a fair amount of time on YouTube, though I'd say that's more a way of unwinding than anything productive. For university I'm constantly digging around on academic databases, which are far less glamorous but infinitely more useful.

questions.question: What types of websites are most popular in your country?
questions.answer: Social media dominates, without question — Telegram and Instagram in particular have an enormous user base here. Online marketplaces have also taken off over the last few years, especially since delivery services improved. What's interesting is that a lot of small businesses now operate entirely through social media rather than building their own sites.

vocab.meaning: a very large number of users

questions.question: What is your favourite website?
questions.answer: Probably Wikipedia, as boring as that sounds. I go on to check one fact and end up falling down a rabbit hole for an hour, reading about something completely unrelated. It's endlessly browsable in a way most sites aren't, and I like that it isn't cluttered with adverts trying to sell me something.

vocab.meaning: get lost following one link after another
vocab.uz: bir mavzudan boshqasiga o'tib ketib, chalg'ib qolmoq

vocab.meaning: you can keep exploring it without getting bored

questions.question: Have the websites you often visit changed over time?
questions.answer: Enormously. As a teenager I lived on gaming sites and forums, whereas now most of my time online is either work-related or news. I've also noticed that I've drifted away from browsing websites at all — almost everything happens through apps these days. In a way I miss the old internet; it felt less algorithm-driven.

vocab.meaning: spend almost all your time there
vocab.uz: u yerdan chiqmaslik, doim o'sha yerda bo'lmoq

practice.question: Do you use websites for studying?
practice.answer: All the time. I dig around on academic sites for articles, and I find online dictionaries infinitely more useful than paper ones, because they show real examples of how a word is used.

practice.question: What makes a website good, in your opinion?
practice.answer: For me, it's a clean design. Nothing puts me off faster than a page cluttered with adverts. Good sites are simple to navigate but also endlessly browsable — you keep finding something new.

practice.question: Do you spend too much time online?
practice.answer: Probably. Browsing is a way of unwinding after classes, but I often fall down a rabbit hole and lose an hour. That's partly why I've drifted away from algorithm-driven feeds and started using bookmarks instead.

questions.question: Do you wear a watch?
questions.answer: I do, though it's more out of habit than necessity. I've got a fairly plain analogue watch that my father gave me, and I feel oddly incomplete without it. I know most people my age have done away with watches entirely and just use their phones, but I quite like having something on my wrist.

vocab.meaning: because you are used to it
strangely as if something is missing

questions.question: What kind of watches do you like?
questions.answer: I'm drawn to understated designs — a plain face, a leather strap, nothing flashy. I find enormous watches with a dozen dials a bit over the top. What matters more to me is that it's built to last; I'd rather buy one decent watch than replace a cheap one every year.

vocab.meaning: showy in a slightly vulgar way

questions.question: How do you usually check the time?
questions.answer: Honestly, my phone — nine times out of ten it's already in my hand. I glance at my watch when I'm in a meeting or a lecture, because pulling your phone out looks rude. And there's something to be said for a watch at a glance; it's quicker than unlocking a screen.

vocab.phrase: there's something to be said for
vocab.meaning: there is a genuine advantage to

questions.question: Have you ever received a watch as a gift?
questions.answer: Yes — the one I wear, in fact. My father gave it to me when I finished school, and it had been his before that, so it carries a lot of sentimental weight. I think watches make a thoughtful gift precisely because they get worn every day. It's not something you shove in a drawer and forget about.

vocab.meaning: something in a drawer put it away carelessly

practice.question: Are watches still useful today?
practice.answer: Less than they used to be. Nine times out of ten, people check their phones instead. Still, I wear one out of habit, and it's handy in exams, where phones aren't allowed.

practice.question: Would you ever buy an expensive watch?
practice.answer: I might, but only a classic, understated one. I don't like anything flashy or over the top — I'd rather spend money on something built to last than on a brand name.

practice.question: Is a watch a good present?
practice.answer: It can be a thoughtful gift if you know the person's style. Otherwise there's a real risk they'll shove it in a drawer and never wear it, which is a shame given what watches cost.

questions.question: Do you like shopping?
questions.answer: It rather depends what for. Shopping for books or food I genuinely enjoy — I can happily lose an hour in a bookshop. Clothes shopping, on the other hand, I find an absolute chore; I go in knowing exactly what I want and I'm out within twenty minutes. I'd never describe it as a leisure activity.

vocab.meaning: enjoyably spend an hour without noticing
something done for enjoyment in free time

questions.question: How often do you go shopping?
questions.answer: For groceries, two or three times a week — I prefer buying fresh things in small amounts rather than doing one big shop. For anything else, very sparingly. I try to hold off on buying something for a week or so, and more often than not I realise I didn't really want it.

vocab.meaning: buy a large amount of groceries at once

questions.question: Do you compare prices when you shop?
questions.answer: Always, for anything expensive. I'll check three or four sites before committing, because prices can vary wildly for exactly the same item. For small purchases I don't bother — the time you spend hunting for a better deal isn't worth the saving. I suppose I'm price-conscious rather than stingy.

vocab.meaning: justified by the money you save

questions.question: Do you find it difficult to make decisions when shopping?
questions.answer: Sometimes, yes — especially when there's an overwhelming amount of choice. Twenty near- identical options make it harder, not easier. What helps me is narrowing it down to two before I go anywhere near the shop. Otherwise I go round in circles and end up buying nothing at all.

vocab.meaning: think about something without making progress
vocab.uz: bir joyda aylanib qolmoq, qaror qila olmaslik

practice.question: Do you prefer shopping online or in shops?
practice.answer: Online, for most things. Going to a shopping centre is an absolute chore for me, especially at weekends. For some people it's a leisure activity, but I'd rather order something and get on with my day.

practice.question: What do you enjoy buying most?
practice.answer: Books, without a doubt. I can happily lose an hour in a bookshop. I buy clothes very sparingly by comparison, and only when I actually need something.

practice.question: Have you ever regretted something you bought?
practice.answer: Occasionally. I once bought a phone on impulse instead of holding off on it until the sales. Now I'm much more price-conscious: I hunt for a better deal and compare reviews to narrow it down before paying.

part1.name: Cars

questions.question: What type of car do you like?
questions.answer: Nothing extravagant — something small, fuel-efficient and easy to park. I'd take reliability over speed every single time. If I'm honest, I've never really understood people who see cars as a status symbol; for me it's simply a means of getting from A to B.

vocab.meaning: something owned to show wealth or rank

vocab.phrase: a means of getting from A to B

questions.question: Does the colour of a car matter to you?
questions.answer: Not hugely, though I'd probably avoid white — it shows every speck of dirt. Darker colours look smarter but they're a nightmare to keep clean as well. Realistically I'd go for grey or dark blue, which is a thoroughly unadventurous answer, but practical.

vocab.uz: har bir chang zarrasi ko'rinib turmoq

questions.question: Do you prefer to be a driver or a passenger?
questions.answer: A passenger, definitely. Driving in the city here requires your full concentration, and I find it genuinely draining in traffic. As a passenger I can read, listen to a podcast or just watch the world go by. That said, I do like driving on open roads where there's no one around.

questions.question: Do you like sitting in the front seat or the back seat?
questions.answer: The front, for the view more than anything. You feel much less cooped up and I'm prone to travel sickness in the back, particularly on winding roads. On long journeys with friends, though, I'd rather sit in the back where you can stretch out and actually talk to everyone.

practice.question: Would you like to have your own car one day?
practice.answer: Eventually, yes, but nothing fancy. I'd want something small and fuel-efficient, and definitely not white — a friend of mine says hers is a nightmare to keep clean.

practice.question: Are cars important to people in your country?
practice.answer: Very. For a lot of people a car is a status symbol, so they'll spend far more than they can afford. For me, it's simply a means of getting from A to B.

practice.question: Do you enjoy long car journeys?
practice.answer: As a passenger, I love them — I can stretch out in the back and watch the world go by. Driving long distances is a different story. It's draining, and I am prone to getting sleepy after a couple of hours.

phraseBank: a means of getting from A to B

questions.question: Do you often visit parks?
questions.answer: As often as I can, especially in spring when the weather's just right. There's a park about ten minutes from my flat and I'll walk there most evenings to clear my head after studying. In winter I go far less — the appeal wears off rather quickly once it's freezing.

vocab.meaning: perfect, neither too much nor too little

questions.question: What do you usually do when you go to a park?
questions.answer: Mostly walk, or sit somewhere with a book. Occasionally I'll go with friends and we'll bring something to eat and just sprawl on the grass for a couple of hours. I'm not one of those people who goes to a park to exercise — I'd rather use it to slow down than speed up.

vocab.meaning: lie or sit in a relaxed way on the grass

questions.question: Are there many parks in your city?
questions.answer: A reasonable number, though they're unevenly distributed — the centre is very well served and the outskirts far less so. Several new ones have opened recently as part of a regeneration scheme, which has made a real difference. Still, compared with some European cities, we're somewhat short on green space.

vocab.meaning: a project to improve an urban area

questions.question: Do you think parks are important in cities? Why?
questions.answer: Absolutely essential, I'd say. They're one of the few genuinely free public spaces left, which matters enormously in a city where everything else costs money. There's also a well- documented link between access to greenery and mental wellbeing. And practically speaking, trees help bring the temperature down in summer, which is no small thing here.

vocab.meaning: an open area anyone can use at no cost
supported by a lot of evidence

practice.question: Did you often go to parks as a child?
practice.answer: Almost every weekend. My parents took us to a park near the river, where we'd sprawl on the grass after running around. As a teenager, the appeal wore off for a while, and I preferred shopping centres.

practice.question: What's your favourite park?
practice.answer: There's a small park near my university that I visit between lectures to clear my head. It's nothing special, but it makes me slow down for twenty minutes, which I really need.

practice.question: Would you like more parks near your home?
practice.answer: Definitely. Parks in my city are very unevenly distributed — the centre is well served, but newer districts are short on them. Given how much research links nature to mental wellbeing, that seems unfair.

questions.question: Do you like science?
questions.answer: I find it fascinating, though I'd never claim to be scientifically minded. I'm the sort of person who loves reading about discoveries without wanting to do the maths behind them. Physics in particular captures my imagination — the idea that a few equations describe the whole universe is extraordinary.

vocab.meaning: having a natural aptitude for science

questions.question: Did you enjoy science lessons as a child?
questions.answer: It depended entirely on the teacher, if I'm honest. We had a biology teacher who did proper experiments and made the whole thing come alive. Chemistry, by contrast, was mostly copying formulas off the board, which put me off the subject for years. Good teaching makes an enormous difference at that age.

vocab.meaning: board write down what the teacher wrote
someone off (a subject) make them lose interest in it

questions.question: Do you enjoy watching science-related videos?
questions.answer: Very much — it's probably how I do most of my learning outside university. There are channels that explain complex ideas in plain language without dumbing them down, and I find that far more engaging than reading a textbook. A good ten-minute video can get a concept across better than an hour-long lecture.

vocab.meaning: oversimplify it to the point of losing meaning

questions.question: Would you like to learn more about science in the future?
questions.answer: Definitely, though on my own terms rather than formally. I don't think I'd go back and study it at degree level, but I'd happily work my way through a few good popular science books. What appeals to me is understanding enough to follow the debate when something significant is discovered.

vocab.meaning: in the way that suits me
understand and keep up with a discussion

practice.question: Which branch of science interests you most?
practice.answer: I'm not especially scientifically minded, but astronomy has always captured my imagination. Anything about how the universe began makes me want to keep reading.

practice.question: Who was your favourite science teacher?
practice.answer: My chemistry teacher in year nine. Lessons really came alive with her, because she did experiments instead of lecturing. The teacher before her had nearly put me off the subject completely.

practice.question: Should science be explained more simply for the public?
practice.answer: Yes, as long as it's explained in plain language rather than dumbed down. The best science YouTubers get complex concepts across without losing accuracy, and people can then explore further on their own terms.

questions.question: Are you interested in outer space and stars?
questions.answer: I am, in an amateur sort of way. I couldn't name more than a handful of constellations, but the sheer scale of it is something I find genuinely humbling. Whenever I read about how far away even the nearest star is, it rather puts everyday problems into perspective.

vocab.phrase: in an amateur sort of way

vocab.meaning: enormous size ulkan miqyos humbling making you feel small and modest
perspective make you see what really matters

questions.question: Do you often watch videos or documentaries about space?
questions.answer: Fairly often, yes — they're my go-to when I want something interesting but undemanding. The photography in modern documentaries is breathtaking, and I like that they manage to explain things without assuming you have a physics degree. I'd say I watch one every few weeks, usually on a whim.

questions.question: Do you enjoy looking at the stars at night?
questions.answer: I love it, but light pollution in the city makes it almost pointless. You might see a dozen stars on a good night. Whenever I go back to my grandparents' village, the sky is absolutely covered in them, and it genuinely stops you in your tracks. It's one of the things I miss most about being out of the city.

vocab.meaning: excess artificial light that hides the stars
tracks make them stop out of amazement

questions.question: Would you like to travel to space if you had the chance?
questions.answer: In theory, absolutely — but I'd want to wait until the technology matures. At the moment it strikes me as an unnecessary risk for a few minutes of weightlessness. If it became as routine as flying, then yes, I'd jump at the chance. Seeing the Earth from above must change how you think about almost everything.

vocab.meaning: something matures wait for it to become more developed

practice.question: Did you learn much about space at school?
practice.answer: Only the basics, unfortunately — the planets and a bit about gravity. What stayed with me was the sheer scale of it all. Realising how tiny Earth is was genuinely humbling.

practice.question: Have you ever been somewhere with a really clear night sky?
practice.answer: Yes, once in the mountains near Chimgan. We drove up on a whim one summer night, and with no light pollution, the sky was absolutely breathtaking. I've never seen so many stars.

practice.question: Should countries spend money on space exploration?
practice.answer: I think so. Space research gave us satellites and accurate weather forecasts, and seeing Earth from above puts our problems into perspective. Space tourism is an unnecessary risk right now, though — even if I'd secretly jump at the chance myself!

questions.question: Do you often use headphones?
questions.answer: Constantly — they're probably the piece of technology I'd struggle most to live without. I use them on the commute, in the library, and even at home when I need to block out background noise. I'm aware that wearing them all day isn't doing my hearing any favours, so I try to keep the volume moderate.

vocab.meaning: find it very hard to manage without

questions.question: What type of headphones do you use?
questions.answer: I've got a pair of over-ear ones with noise cancellation, which were an extravagance but absolutely worth it. I also keep cheap earbuds in my bag as a backup, because there's nothing worse than a dead battery on a long journey. The over-ear ones are far more comfortable for extended periods.

vocab.meaning: in reserve, in case of problems

questions.question: Do you prefer wireless or wired headphones? Why?
questions.answer: Wireless, mainly for convenience — not being tethered to your phone makes a bigger difference than you'd expect. The obvious downside is that they run out of charge at the worst possible moment. Audio purists would argue wired is better quality, and they're probably right, but I doubt my ears are discerning enough to notice.

vocab.uz: nozik farqni sezadigan, tanqidiy did bilan

questions.question: In what situations do you not use headphones?
questions.answer: Never when I'm crossing roads or cycling — that's simply asking for trouble. I also take them out whenever I'm with other people, because leaving one in is quietly rude even if you can still hear them. And I find I can't wear them while reading anything difficult; the music competes for my attention.

vocab.meaning: behave in a way that invites danger
distract me from what I'm doing

practice.question: When did you first start using headphones?
practice.answer: In secondary school, on the long bus ride home. Now I honestly struggle to live without them — they're the only way to block out the noise on the metro, so I panic slightly when they run out of charge.

practice.question: Can headphones be bad for your hearing?
practice.answer: They can be if you wear them for extended periods at high volume. That's one reason I bought a pair with noise cancellation. It felt like an extravagance at the time, but I no longer need to turn the volume up.

practice.question: Is it rude to wear headphones when you're with other people?
practice.answer: In a conversation, definitely. Even keeping one earbud in is quietly rude. And wearing them while cycling in city traffic is just asking for trouble.

part1.name: Singing

questions.question: Do you like singing? Why?
questions.answer: I do, though almost exclusively when nobody's listening — in the shower or in the car. There's something about it that lifts you out of a bad mood almost immediately. I think it's the breathing as much as the music; you can't sing properly and stay tense at the same time.

vocab.phrase: lift someone out of a bad

questions.question: Did you enjoy singing when you were a child?
questions.answer: Enormously — I was in the school choir for about three years and I loved every minute of it. What I remember most isn't the performances but the rehearsals, when forty voices suddenly clicked into place. I stopped when I hit my teens and got self-conscious about it, which I regret now.

vocab.uz: uyala boshlamoq, o'zini noqulay his qilmoq

questions.question: Are you good at singing?
questions.answer: I'd say I can hold a tune, which is about as far as I'd go. I'm not going to be troubling any talent shows, but I don't make people wince either. My sister is the genuinely musical one in the family — she got the voice and I got the enthusiasm.

vocab.meaning: trouble any talent shows be nowhere near professional standard

questions.question: Do you think singing lifts people's mood?
questions.answer: Without a doubt, and there's research to back that up. Singing together in particular seems to create a strong sense of connection — you see it at concerts and at weddings alike. I'd also say it's one of the few activities where being bad at it doesn't diminish the enjoyment in the slightest.

vocab.meaning: a feeling of closeness to others

practice.question: Do you ever sing karaoke?
practice.answer: Very rarely. I get self-conscious about singing in front of people, and honestly, I can barely hold a tune. I mostly sing in the car when nobody's listening.

practice.question: Is singing popular at celebrations in your country?
practice.answer: Enormously — no Uzbek wedding is complete without it. Even people whose singing would make you wince join in, and nobody minds in the slightest. It creates a sense of connection between the guests.

practice.question: Would you like to take singing lessons?
practice.answer: Maybe just for fun. I'm realistic — I'm never going to trouble any talent shows. But singing always lifts me out of a bad mood, so a few lessons might make it even more enjoyable.

phraseBank: lift someone out of a bad mood

part1.name: Zoos

questions.question: Do you like going to zoos?
questions.answer: I have mixed feelings about them, to be honest. As a day out they're enjoyable, and there's no substitute for seeing an animal in the flesh. But I often come away feeling slightly uncomfortable about the enclosures. I'd much rather visit a proper wildlife park where the animals have room to roam.

questions.question: Did you often visit a zoo when you were a child?
questions.answer: Reasonably often — it was one of those places parents take you when they've run out of ideas for the weekend. I remember being completely transfixed by the big cats. Looking back, I suspect I enjoyed the ice cream and the day out just as much as the animals themselves.

vocab.meaning: be unable to look away from

questions.question: What animals do you like to see in zoos?
questions.answer: Anything I'd never come across otherwise — snow leopards, elephants, that sort of thing. I'm less interested in the animals you could see in any field. Primates are particularly compelling because their behaviour is unnervingly familiar; you can watch them for an hour and forget you're in a zoo at all.

vocab.meaning: similar in a way that is slightly disturbing

questions.question: Do you think zoos are good for animals?
questions.answer: It cuts both ways. The best zoos do serious conservation work and have brought species back from the brink of extinction, which is genuinely valuable. But plenty of others keep animals in conditions that are frankly indefensible. So I don't think you can generalise — it depends entirely on how well the place is run.

vocab.meaning: have both advantages and disadvantages ikki tomonlama, ham foydasi ham zarari bor bring something back from the brink save it from disappearing
make a broad statement about everything

practice.question: Is there a zoo in your city?
practice.answer: Yes, Tashkent has quite a big one. I went last year with my nephew, who was transfixed by the giraffes for twenty minutes. Seeing them in the flesh is very different from watching them on a screen.

practice.question: Would you take your own children to a zoo?
practice.answer: Probably, though I have mixed feelings about it. Good zoos give animals room to roam and help bring species back from the brink. But keeping big cats in small cages is frankly indefensible.

practice.question: Do you prefer seeing animals in the wild or in zoos?
practice.answer: In the wild, if I could afford it. Documentaries are compelling, but you miss the smell and the noise. Zoos are a compromise, and like most compromises, the argument cuts both ways.

phraseBank: bring something back from the brink

questions.question: Are there many wild animals in your country?
questions.answer: There are, though most people never see them because they're concentrated in the mountains and the desert regions. We've got snow leopards in the highlands, which are famously elusive, and a fair amount of birdlife around the lakes. Sadly, quite a few species are now under threat as their habitat gets squeezed by farming.

vocab.meaning: very hard to find or see
the birds of a particular area
be gradually reduced or pushed out

questions.question: Do you like watching programmes about wild animals?
questions.answer: I do — nature documentaries are one of the few things I'll watch from start to finish without reaching for my phone. The camerawork alone is worth it; some of the footage they capture is astonishing. What I appreciate most is that they usually strike a balance between entertaining you and making a serious point about conservation.

vocab.meaning: all the way through boshidan oxirigacha footage recorded film material video lavha, tasvir astonishing extremely impressive or surprising

questions.question: What is your favourite wild animal?
questions.answer: The snow leopard, without hesitation — partly because it's native to our mountains and partly because it's so rarely seen. There's something appealing about an animal that keeps its distance from people. I've only ever seen one in footage, but it moves through that terrain with extraordinary grace.

vocab.meaning: naturally live in a particular place
vocab.uz: o'sha yerga xos bo'lmoq, tub aholisi bo'lmoq

vocab.meaning: an area of land and its physical features yer yuzasi, relyef grace smooth and elegant movement

questions.question: Do you think wild animals should be protected?
questions.answer: Unquestionably, though I think the argument is often made badly. People tend to focus on how beautiful a species is, when the stronger case is that ecosystems unravel once you remove a predator. There's also a straightforward economic argument — wildlife tourism brings in real money. Protection isn't sentimentality; it's self-interest.

vocab.meaning: an animal that hunts others yirtqich hayvon bring in (money) generate income
excessive emotion, softness haddan ortiq hissiyot self-interest acting for your own benefit

practice.question: Have you ever seen a wild animal up close?
practice.answer: Once, on a hike in the mountains, I saw a fox. It kept its distance from us, of course, but for a few seconds we just stared at each other. It was a surprisingly moving moment.

practice.question: Is there an animal that is special to your country?
practice.answer: The snow leopard. It is native to our mountain ranges, but it's so elusive that most Uzbeks have never seen one. The rugged terrain helps it hide, but like many species it is under threat from poaching.

practice.question: Should people be allowed to keep wild animals as pets?
practice.answer: I don't think so. A predator belongs in the wild, however well it's treated at home. Eco-tourism is a far better option — it brings in money for local communities and helps strike a balance between people and nature.

questions.question: Do you like flowers?
questions.answer: Very much, though I appreciate them more growing than in a vase. There's a park near me that's a riot of colour in April, and I'll deliberately take the longer route home just to walk through it. Cut flowers I find slightly sad — they look wonderful for three days and then you're throwing them out.

vocab.meaning: an impressive display of many bright colours
flowers picked and sold in bunches

questions.question: What types of flowers do you like most?
questions.answer: Roses, predictably — Namangan is well known for them, so I grew up around them. Beyond that I'm fond of tulips, mostly because they're the first thing to appear after winter and they feel like a sign that spring has arrived. I'm less keen on the heavily scented varieties; lilies in particular are overpowering indoors.

vocab.meaning: something be surrounded by it in childhood

questions.question: Have you ever given flowers to someone?
questions.answer: Plenty of times — it's practically obligatory here for birthdays and for the first of September. I gave my mother a bunch of roses last spring for no particular reason, and I think that went down far better than any of the ones I've given on official occasions. Unexpected flowers carry more weight.

vocab.meaning: a bundle of flowers bir dasta go down well be received positively

questions.question: Have you ever received flowers as a gift?
questions.answer: Once or twice, though it's much less common for men here, so it caught me off guard the first time. A friend brought some when I moved into my flat, which was a lovely touch. I'll admit I had no idea what to do with them — I ended up improvising a vase out of a water bottle.

vocab.meaning: surprise them when they are unprepared
of make it from whatever is available

practice.question: Are flowers popular in your country?
practice.answer: Very. In spring the city parks are a riot of colour, especially when the tulips come out. People are fond of roses too — lots of families grow a few in the yard.

practice.question: Do you keep any plants or flowers at home?
practice.answer: My mum keeps pots of basil and geraniums on the balcony. I love scented flowers in general, although some, like lilies, can be a bit overpowering in a small room.

practice.question: When do people in your country give flowers?
practice.answer: On birthdays, Women's Day and graduations, mainly. A bunch of tulips always goes down well. Giving flowers for no reason at all can really catch someone off guard, which is a lovely touch.

questions.question: Do you often visit the countryside?
questions.answer: Not as often as I'd like — realistically two or three times a year, usually to see relatives in the village. Whenever I do go, I wonder why I don't make the effort more often. It only takes a couple of hours to get there, so there's no real excuse beyond being caught up in everything else.

vocab.meaning: take the trouble to do something
there is no genuine reason not to

questions.question: Why is the countryside more peaceful?
questions.answer: The obvious reason is the absence of traffic — you don't realise how much background noise you've been tuning out until it's gone. But I think it's also the pace; nobody seems to be in a hurry there. And there's far less visual clutter, no advertising or flashing signs competing for your attention.

vocab.meaning: too many things to look at
attention all demand to be noticed

questions.question: Is there anything interesting in the countryside?
questions.answer: Plenty, though it's a slower kind of interesting. You won't find museums or nightlife, but there are ruins and old mosques dotted around that almost nobody visits. The food is a genuine draw as well — everything is grown locally and it tastes noticeably better. And the night sky alone is worth the journey.

questions.question: Would you like to live in the countryside in the future?
questions.answer: Possibly later in life, but not now. At my age I'd find it isolating — the career opportunities simply aren't there, and I'd miss having everything on my doorstep. In my fifties, though, I can absolutely picture it. I think a lot of people romanticise rural life until they actually try a winter there.

vocab.meaning: making you feel cut off from others
very close to where you live
imagine something as better than it is

practice.question: What do you do when you go to the countryside?
practice.answer: Mostly nothing, which is the point! I help my grandparents in the orchard and eat fruit grown locally. It's the only time I'm not caught up in deadlines and messages.

practice.question: Did you spend time in the countryside as a child?
practice.answer: Every summer. My grandparents' village had little farms dotted around the hills. Coming home, I'd suddenly notice all the background noise of the city that I usually tune out.

practice.question: Is life in the countryside easier than city life?
practice.answer: Not really. People tend to romanticise it, but there are fewer jobs and hospitals. I love having nature on my doorstep for a few days, though, and I should make the effort to go more often.

questions.question: How do people usually improve their memory?
questions.answer: The most effective method seems to be testing yourself rather than simply rereading things — recalling something is what makes it stick. A lot of people also swear by mnemonics, associating information with vivid images. And the unglamorous answer is sleep; you consolidate most of what you've learned overnight.

vocab.meaning: check what you can recall without looking
make it stay in your memory
believe strongly in the effectiveness of

questions.question: Are you good at remembering people's names?
questions.answer: I'm notoriously bad at it, unfortunately. I can remember an entire conversation with someone and still draw a complete blank on their name five minutes later. I've started repeating the name back when I'm introduced, which helps a little, but it's still something I have to work at consciously.

vocab.uz: esga tushira olmaslik, xayoli bo'shab qolmoq

vocab.meaning: something consciously make a deliberate effort

questions.question: Have you ever forgotten something really important?
questions.answer: Once, memorably — I forgot a friend's birthday entirely, and only realised when I saw the photographs the next day. I felt dreadful about it. Since then I've put everything in my calendar with a reminder, because I've accepted that I simply can't rely on my own memory for dates.

vocab.meaning: something feel very guilty or bad about it
something in the calendar schedule it so you don't forget

questions.question: Do you find it easy to memorize new things?
questions.answer: It depends enormously on whether it interests me. Anything I can connect to something I already know goes in almost effortlessly. Arbitrary information — phone numbers, dates, lists of names — is a different matter entirely; that requires sheer repetition and it still slips away within a week.

vocab.meaning: something to what you already know link new information to existing knowledge
without any difficulty hech qiynalmasdan sheer repetition nothing but repeating over and over

practice.question: Is your memory better now than when you were a child?
practice.answer: Probably worse! As a kid I learned whole poems through sheer repetition. Now I have to test myself with flashcards to make new vocabulary stick.

practice.question: What kind of things do you find hard to remember?
practice.answer: Dates and birthdays. I'm notoriously bad at them — I once drew a blank when someone asked me my own sister's birthday, which was embarrassing.

practice.question: Do you use your phone to help you remember things?
practice.answer: Constantly. I rely on reminders for everything, and a friend of mine swears by a notes app. The risk is that we stop training our memory, and small details simply slip away.

questions.question: What kinds of landscapes are common in your country?
questions.answer: It's remarkably varied for a country of its size. Much of it is arid steppe and desert, particularly in the west, but the east is dominated by mountains that are snow-capped for most of the year. In between you've got the valleys, which are lush and heavily cultivated — almost a different country entirely.

questions.question: Do you think landscapes are important for tourism?
questions.answer: They're absolutely central to it. People will travel a very long way for scenery they can't see at home, and mountains in particular draw enormous numbers of visitors. The challenge is managing that properly — unchecked development can ruin the very thing people came to see, which would be shooting yourself in the foot.

questions.question: Do you enjoy taking photos of landscapes?
questions.answer: I do, though I've largely made my peace with the fact that the photo never does justice to what you actually saw. A phone camera flattens everything out and you lose all the depth. These days I take one or two and then put the phone away — I'd rather remember the place than the photograph.

vocab.meaning: represent it as well as it deserves
vocab.uz: asl holicha aks ettirmoq, haqqini bermoq

vocab.meaning: make it lose depth and dimension

questions.question: What views can you see from the windows of your home?
questions.answer: Nothing dramatic, unfortunately — mainly rooftops and the building opposite. From the kitchen there's a slice of park visible between two blocks, which is the closest thing I get to a view. On very clear days the mountains appear on the horizon, and it's a genuine treat when they do.

vocab.phrase: the closest thing I get to

practice.question: What's your favourite type of landscape?
practice.answer: Mountains, definitely. Most of Uzbekistan is flat and arid, so seeing snow-capped peaks is always a genuine treat for me.

practice.question: Have you ever travelled somewhere just for the scenery?
practice.answer: Yes — we once drove to the Fergana Valley in spring, when everything was green and lush. I took hundreds of photos, but none did justice to the view, so eventually I just put the phone away.

practice.question: Is it important to protect natural landscapes?
practice.answer: Very. Beautiful places draw large numbers of tourists, which helps the economy, but unchecked development can ruin exactly what people came to see.

questions.question: Are you good at telling jokes?
questions.answer: Not remotely, no. I can never get the timing right and I have a terrible habit of laughing before I reach the punchline, which ruins it completely. I'm much better at being the audience. My humour tends to be situational rather than joke-based — I'm funnier by accident than on purpose.

vocab.meaning: deliver something at exactly the right moment
the final funny part of a joke

questions.question: Do your friends like to tell jokes?
questions.answer: Constantly — one of them in particular is a natural storyteller and can hold a room for twenty minutes. The rest of us mostly wind each other up, which is a different kind of humour but arguably funnier. I think that sort of teasing is a sign of how comfortable a group is with one another.

vocab.meaning: someone with an instinctive gift for telling stories

questions.question: Do you enjoy watching comedies?
questions.answer: They're my default choice when I want to switch off. I'd take a good sitcom over a serious drama on a weeknight any day of the week. What I've noticed is that comedy travels badly — a lot of humour depends on cultural references, so shows that are hilarious at home can fall completely flat elsewhere.

questions.question: Have you ever watched a live comedy show?
questions.answer: Once, at a small venue with a stand-up comedian, and it was a completely different experience from watching on a screen. The atmosphere is infectious — you laugh far harder simply because everyone around you is. What impressed me most was how he played off the audience and improvised half the set.

vocab.meaning: a place where an event is held
react to and use the crowd's responses
vocab.uz: tomoshabinlar bilan o'ynab, ularga moslashib ketmoq

practice.question: Who is the funniest person you know?
practice.answer: My uncle. He's a natural storyteller and can hold a room at any family dinner. He never rushes a joke — he always gets the timing right.

practice.question: Are jokes in other languages hard to understand?
practice.answer: Often, yes. Wordplay in English sometimes falls flat for me, because I only get the punchline after someone explains it — and by then it's not funny anymore.

practice.question: What kind of TV shows make you laugh?
practice.answer: Sitcoms are my default choice after a long day. I also love shows where comedians improvise, because the energy is so infectious — you laugh even when the jokes aren't perfect.

questions.question: How often do you use social media?
questions.answer: Far more than I'd like, if I'm being honest — my screen time report is a sobering read every Sunday. I've started putting limits on the worst apps, which helps a little. The problem is that it's become so woven into everyday life that avoiding it entirely isn't really practical.

vocab.meaning: something that makes you think seriously
restrict how much you use something

questions.question: What do you usually use social media for?
questions.answer: Mainly keeping in touch with people I don't see often — old school friends, relatives abroad. I also follow a fair few accounts related to my studies, which is genuinely useful. What I don't do much of is posting; I'm very much a lurker rather than someone who documents their life online.

vocab.meaning: someone who reads but never posts
vocab.uz: faqat kuzatib yuradigan, hech narsa yozmaydigan foydalanuvchi

vocab.meaning: record and share what you do

questions.question: What is the most popular social media platform in your country?
questions.answer: Telegram, without any real competition. It's used for absolutely everything here — not just messaging but news channels, shopping, even paying for things. Instagram comes second and is where most small businesses showcase their products. What's striking is how quickly platforms can fall out of favour; Facebook has almost vanished among younger people.

vocab.meaning: display something to its best advantage

practice.question: Do you post a lot on social media?
practice.answer: Hardly ever. I'm more of a lurker — I read, but rarely post. Some people document their whole lives online, but I prefer to keep things private.

practice.question: Has social media changed the way you communicate?
practice.answer: Completely. It is woven into everyday life now, and it's how I keep in touch with friends who moved abroad. Facebook has fallen out of favour here, though — it's all Telegram and Instagram now.

practice.question: Do you spend too much time on social media?
practice.answer: Probably. My weekly screen-time report is a sobering read! I've started to put limits on certain apps. I still use Instagram to showcase my photography, but I try not to scroll aimlessly.

questions.question: Do you like sitting in one place for a long time?
questions.answer: Not particularly — I get restless after about forty minutes and need to move. I've found that I concentrate far better if I get up and stretch every hour rather than trying to sit through a four- hour session. Sitting still for too long leaves me feeling sluggish rather than focused.

vocab.meaning: unable to stay still or relax
endure it from beginning to end

questions.question: What do you usually do when you sit?
questions.answer: It's usually study or reading, so I'm hunched over a laptop more often than not. In the evenings I sit with a book, which is a completely different posture and far more comfortable. When I'm with friends we mostly sit and talk — nothing more elaborate than that.

vocab.meaning: the way you hold your body

vocab.uz: shundan boshqa hech qanday murakkab narsa yo'q

questions.question: What's your favourite place to sit?
questions.answer: There's an armchair by the window in my flat that gets the afternoon sun, and that's where I end up whenever I've got a free hour. It's nothing special to look at, but it's worn in in exactly the right way. I'd say it's the one spot in the house where I properly switch off.

vocab.meaning: stop thinking about things and relax

questions.question: When you were a child, did you like sitting on the floor?
questions.answer: Always — I don't think I sat on a chair unless I was made to. That's fairly standard practice here anyway; we eat sitting on the floor around a low table, so it never felt unusual. I can still manage it for an hour or so, though I'll admit my knees protest more than they used to.

vocab.meaning: the normal, usual way of doing things odatiy holat, an'anaviy tartib unless I was made to unless I was forced to

practice.question: How many hours a day do you spend sitting?
practice.answer: Far too many — probably ten, between lectures and studying. By the evening I feel sluggish, and I know my posture suffers because I'm hunched over a laptop.

practice.question: Do you find it hard to sit still in long lectures?
practice.answer: Yes, I get restless after about forty minutes. Sitting through a three-hour lecture is tough, so I always get up and stretch during the break.

practice.question: Where do you like to sit when you want to relax?
practice.answer: On our balcony. It gets the afternoon sun, and with a cup of tea I can properly switch off for half an hour.

questions.question: Do you like advertisements that appear on TV?
questions.answer: As a rule, no — they interrupt the flow of whatever you're watching, which is precisely why streaming has become so popular. That said, I'll happily admit that a genuinely clever advert can be more entertaining than the programme. The ones I object to are the relentlessly repetitive ones that run every single break.

questions.question: What do you usually do when you see advertisements on TV?
questions.answer: Reach for my phone, almost automatically — which rather defeats the purpose of the advert. Sometimes I'll use the break to put the kettle on or do something useful. If it's something I've already seen a dozen times, I'll mute it without even thinking about it.

questions.question: Do you dislike any type of advertisement?
questions.answer: The ones that prey on people's insecurities — anything implying you're inadequate unless you buy the product. I find that genuinely distasteful. I'm also not keen on adverts aimed at young children, who aren't old enough to recognise that they're being sold to. Beyond that, I've largely learned to tune them out.

vocab.uz: e'tibor bermay qo'ymoq, o'zini eshitmaganga solmoq

practice.question: Do you remember any adverts from your childhood?
practice.answer: Yes — a juice advert with a terribly catchy jingle. It was relentlessly repetitive, so the whole country could sing it. It's funny how I still remember it twenty years later.

practice.question: Are online adverts more annoying than TV adverts?
practice.answer: Much more. On TV you can simply mute them or tune them out, but online they pop up and interrupt the flow of whatever you're reading. Some also prey on people's insecurities, which I find distasteful.

practice.question: Have you ever bought something because of an advert?
practice.answer: As a rule, no — I read reviews instead. But I admit I sometimes reach for a snack brand I've seen advertised when I'm in a hurry.

part2.topic: Describe an ancient city in your country that you would like to visit.
bullets: why you would like to visit it
and explain what you would like to do there
part2.answer: I'd like to talk about Khiva, which sits in the far west of Uzbekistan, not far from the border with Turkmenistan. It's roughly a thousand kilometres from where I live, and that distance is probably the main reason I still haven't been, despite meaning to for years. What I know about it comes mostly from photographs and from a documentary I watched last winter. The old part of the city, Itchan Kala, is completely enclosed by mud-brick walls, and apparently it has been so well preserved that walking through it feels like stepping back several centuries. It was a major stop on the Silk Road, so for hundreds of years traders passed through carrying goods between China and Persia. There's an unfinished minaret there, the Kalta Minor, which was meant to be the tallest in the region until the ruler died before it was completed.
