It now stands as a wide, turquoise stump, and I find that story oddly appealing. The reason I want to go is partly that I've become slightly embarrassed about knowing more about European cities than about my own country. Foreign tourists travel thousands of miles to see Khiva while I've never got round to taking a four-hour flight. If I did go, I'd want to stay inside the walls overnight rather than doing it as a day trip. From what I've read, the place empties out once the tour buses leave, and I imagine seeing those courtyards lit up at night with hardly anyone around would be worth the journey on its own.

vocab.meaning: although you have intended to do it for a long time
vocab.uz: necha yildan beri niyat qilib yurgan bo'lsam-da

vocab.uz: bir necha asr ortga qaytgandek bo'lmoq

vocab.meaning: attractive in a way that is hard to explain

vocab.uz: bir kunlik sayohat qilib qo'ya qolmoq

part2.name: Ancient City

practice.topic: Describe a historical place in your country that you have visited.
bullets: and explain how you felt about the visit
practice.answer: I'd like to talk about Shakhrisabz, the birthplace of Amir Temur, which is about two hours south of Samarkand. I finally visited it last spring, despite meaning to for years. We only did it as a day trip, driving over the mountain pass early in the morning, which was spectacular in itself. The first thing we saw was the ruins of Ak-Saray, Temur's summer palace. Only the gateway is still standing, but the tilework is so well preserved that you can easily imagine how enormous the palace once was. Wandering through the old quarter, with its craftsmen and tiny mosques, really felt like stepping back several centuries. Honestly, I found the place oddly appealing. It isn't as polished as Samarkand, and there's something honest about a monument that's half in ruins. By late afternoon the tour groups had left and the square emptied out, and sitting there as the sun went down was worth the journey on its own. My only regret is that I didn't get round to going sooner.

part2.topic: Describe a time when you answered a stranger's phone call in public.
bullets: and explain how you felt about the situation
part2.answer: This happened about two years ago, on a Saturday afternoon in a park near my office. I'd sat down on a bench to eat my lunch and noticed a phone lying at the other end of it — somebody had clearly left it behind. I was still debating whether to hand it in to a security guard when it started ringing. I answered it mainly because I assumed whoever was calling would know the owner, and that turned out to be exactly right. It was the man's daughter. She'd already worked out that he'd lost it, because he had rung her from a shop's landline about ten minutes earlier. The call itself was fairly chaotic. She was speaking very fast, half in Uzbek and half in Russian, and I kept having to interrupt to explain who I was and where the phone actually was. At one point she seemed to think I was trying to sell it back to her, which was awkward, but we sorted that out soon enough. In the end she asked me to stay put, and her father turned up about fifteen minutes later, completely out of breath. Looking back, I felt good about it, although it was a strange few minutes. There's something oddly intimate about answering somebody else's phone — you're suddenly in the middle of a conversation that has nothing to do with you. What struck me most was how relieved the man was over what was, objectively, just a piece of hardware. I suppose our phones carry far more than we tend to realise.

vocab.meaning: forget to take it with you
think carefully about whether to do it
prove to be, in the end
what impressed or surprised me most

part2.name: A Phone Call

practice.topic: Describe a time when you helped a stranger.
bullets: and explain how you felt afterwards
practice.answer: A few months ago I was on the metro when I noticed that a woman had left her bag behind on the seat as she hurried off at Chorsu. The doors closed before I could say anything, so I debated whether to hand it to a station attendant or try to find her myself. I got off at the next stop, and luckily her phone started ringing inside the bag. The caller turned out to be her husband, who told me she was already heading back. He asked me to stay put on the platform, and ten minutes later she appeared, completely out of breath from running between stations. At first she thought I worked for the metro, which caused a moment of confusion, but we sorted it out quickly and she thanked me about twenty times. I felt great for the rest of the day. What struck me most was how small the effort was on my part compared with how much it meant to her. It made me realise that most people will help if they're given the chance.

part2.topic: Describe a time when you had to listen to someone even though you weren't
bullets: and explain how you felt about having to listen to them
part2.answer: interested in what they were saying. You should say: The occasion I've chosen was a cousin's wedding last summer. I was seated at a table with relatives I barely knew, and one of them — a man in his sixties, some sort of distant uncle — spent the best part of an hour talking to me about the property market. He went into extraordinary detail. He explained what land had cost in his district twenty years ago compared with today, which neighbourhoods had gone up in value, what he'd paid for his own house and what he believed it was worth now. Every so often he'd take out his phone to show me a listing. I wasn't interested for two reasons. The first is simply that I'm a teacher in my twenties with no realistic prospect of buying property any time soon, so almost none of it applied to me. The second is that he wasn't really having a conversation — he was delivering a monologue, and my only job was to nod in the right places. Honestly, I felt trapped. I couldn't leave without being rude, and at a family event you can hardly invent an excuse and walk off. So I sat there, made encouraging noises and quietly kept an eye on the time. That said, I've thought about it rather differently since. He had just retired, and I suspect he didn't have a great many people left to talk to. In hindsight, an hour of my attention wasn't much to give, even if it felt like a very long hour at the time.

vocab.phrase: the best part of an hour

vocab.meaning: talk at length without letting others speak

part2.name: Listening

practice.topic: Describe a lecture or talk that you found boring.
bullets: and explain what you did during it
practice.answer: The one that comes to mind is a guest lecture at my university last year about tax rules for small businesses. Attendance was compulsory, so about two hundred of us squeezed into the main hall. The speaker, a retired official, delivered a monologue for the best part of an hour without a single slide. He went into extraordinary detail about regulations that had changed in the nineties, and there was no realistic prospect of any of us ever needing that information. I found it boring mainly because there was no interaction at all. He never asked a question, and nobody dared to interrupt. Sitting in the middle of a row, I genuinely felt trapped, since leaving would have meant climbing over ten people. So I did what everyone else did: I nodded, made encouraging noises whenever he looked my way, and quietly planned my weekend. In hindsight, I feel slightly guilty, because he'd clearly prepared for weeks. But it taught me a lot about what not to do in my own presentations.

part2.topic: Describe a person you have never lived with but would like to live with.
part2.answer: I'd like to describe my closest friend, Dilnoza, who I've never actually lived with but who I think would make an ideal flatmate. We met at university during our first week — we were assigned to the same seminar group — and we've been close ever since, which is roughly seven years now. We've travelled together several times and once shared a hotel room for a fortnight in Turkey without a single argument, which I'd say is a fairly reliable test. She moved to Almaty for work eighteen months ago, so at the moment it isn't remotely possible. It isn't out of the question in the longer term, though. She's said more than once that she'd like to come back once she's saved enough, and I'm not tied to my current job, so in principle either of us could move. The reason I'd want to live with her is that she's that rare combination of tidy and relaxed. Most people are one or the other. She'll wash up straight away without turning it into a rule that everybody else has to follow. She's also very good at knowing when to leave you alone, which I suspect matters more in a shared flat than being sociable does. Beyond all the practical considerations, I simply miss having somebody to talk to at the end of the day. Messages aren't the same thing at all. Living together would mean the friendship happened in passing rather than having to be arranged in advance, and that's what appeals to me most.

vocab.meaning: a perfect person to share a flat with ideal hamxona be assigned to be officially placed in a group

naturally, as part of everyday life

part2.name: Living Together

practice.topic: Describe a person you have shared a room or home with.
bullets: when and where you lived together
what it was like living with them
and explain whether you would live with them again
practice.answer: I'd like to talk about Jasur, who I shared a room with in my first year at university. We were assigned to the same dormitory room, so we met for the first time on moving day, which was a bit nerve-racking. It turned out he was almost an ideal flatmate. He was quiet in the mornings, he always washed up straight after eating, and he never borrowed anything without asking. The only issue was that he got up at six and I studied late, but we worked around it with an eye mask and a lot of patience. We lived together for about ten months. After that he moved back to Namangan because his family needed help with their business, and now he's tied to that job, so we only see each other occasionally. Would I live with him again? In principle, absolutely. In practice, it's out of the question for now, since we live in different cities. But he mentioned in passing last month that he might move to Tashkent, so who knows?

part2.topic: Describe a decision that was difficult to accept at first but led to a good
bullets: why it was difficult to accept
and explain why you think it was a good decision
part2.answer: outcome in the end. You should say: The decision I want to describe was made by my parents rather than by me, which is partly why it was so hard to swallow. When I was seventeen I'd set my heart on studying in Tashkent and I'd already been accepted. Two months before term began, my father lost his job, and they told me I would have to attend the university in our own city and live at home instead. I took it very badly. I felt I'd worked for two years for nothing, and I was convinced my life was effectively over at seventeen, which is the sort of thing you genuinely believe at that age. I barely spoke to my parents for a fortnight. What actually happened bore no resemblance to what I'd feared. The department in my hometown turned out to be small — about thirty of us — and because of that I got far more attention from the lecturers than I ever would have done in a class of two hundred. One of them took me on as a research assistant in my second year, which I'm certain wouldn't have happened elsewhere. Living at home also saved an enormous amount of money, which meant I could afford a master's later on. Looking back, I think it was the right outcome, even though it was forced on us rather than chosen. I'd have had three more exciting years in Tashkent, but I'd have come out with less at the end of them. It taught me that a setback and a disaster are not the same thing.

vocab.uz: qabul qilish og'ir, hazm qilib bo'lmaydigan

part2.name: Tough Decision

practice.topic: Describe a time when someone else made an important decision for you.
bullets: and explain whether you think it was the right decision
practice.answer: When I finished school, I had set my heart on studying architecture. My parents, however, decided I should study economics instead, mainly because my uncle had offered to take me on at his firm after graduation. I'll admit I took it badly. It felt as if the decision had been forced on me, and for months I barely talked to them about university. It was especially hard to swallow because two of my closest friends were starting architecture that year. Things changed in my second year, though. I discovered that economics bore no resemblance to the dull, number-crunching subject I'd imagined — it was really about people and choices. I also realised I'd liked the idea of architecture more than the work itself. So looking back, I think they made the right call. What felt like a setback at eighteen turned out to be a turning point. When I told my dad that last year, he came out with a very satisfied "I told you so."

part2.topic: Describe a time when you were extremely busy.
bullets: and explain how you felt at the time
part2.answer: The busiest I have ever been was the fortnight leading up to Navruz two years ago. I run a small bakery with my sister, and that period is comfortably our biggest of the year. We were taking orders for holiday breads and sweets on top of our ordinary daily production. Normally we'd bake from about five in the morning until two in the afternoon. During that fortnight we were starting at three and often still packing orders at ten at night. On the busiest single day we produced roughly four times our usual volume. Alongside the baking I was answering the phone, which never stopped, and trying to keep track of who had paid a deposit and who hadn't. The reason it got so out of hand was that we had accepted more orders than we could realistically manage. We'd had a difficult winter financially and I was reluctant to turn anyone away, so I kept saying yes. That was a mistake, and it's one I've since corrected — we now cap the number of orders we take. At the time I honestly felt as though I was running on empty. I was short-tempered with my sister in a way I still regret, and I remember falling asleep at the kitchen table one evening still wearing my apron. There was a strange satisfaction in it too, though. When we finished the final order I felt genuinely proud of what the two of us had managed, and financially that fortnight carried us through the following three months.

part2.name: Busy Time

practice.topic: Describe a time when you worked very hard to finish something.
bullets: why you had to work so hard
and explain how you felt when you finished
practice.answer: I'm going to talk about my graduation thesis, which I finished about a year ago. The real crunch came in the fortnight leading up to the deadline, when my supervisor asked me to rewrite a whole chapter. On top of that, I was working part-time at a café and didn't want to let my manager down. I made a huge spreadsheet to keep track of every section, and I started getting up at six to write before my shift. Friends kept inviting me out, and I had to turn them away every time, which felt awful. There were moments when things nearly got out of hand. At one point I lost two days' work because I hadn't backed it up, and I honestly thought I'd miss the deadline. By the final week I was running on empty, surviving on coffee and about four hours' sleep. What carried me through was my mum, who brought me food and refused to let me give up. When I finally submitted it, I felt relieved more than happy — and then I slept for twelve hours straight.

part2.topic: Describe a person who enjoys taking photos.
bullets: what kind of photos they like taking
when and where they usually take photos
and explain why they enjoy taking photos
part2.answer: The person I'd like to describe is my younger brother, Rustam, who is nineteen and has been obsessed with photography since he was about fourteen. He's almost exclusively interested in people rather than landscapes, which is unusual for somebody of his age. He takes candid portraits — market traders, old men playing chess in the park, children messing about in the street. He's not remotely interested in the kind of polished image you'd see on Instagram; he'd much rather capture somebody mid-gesture, slightly out of focus, than pose them properly. He shoots almost everything in black and white, which he claims strips away the distractions. He goes out most weekends, usually early, because he insists the light is better and there are fewer people about. The old bazaar is his favourite spot — he's been going there so regularly for years that half the traders now know him by name and no longer mind the camera, which is precisely why his photographs of them look so unguarded. As for why he enjoys it, I think there are two things going on. The obvious one is that he's naturally observant; he notices things the rest of us walk straight past. The less obvious one is that photography gives him an excuse to talk to strangers, which he'd otherwise find difficult. He's quite a shy person, but with a camera in his hands he'll happily approach anybody. In a sense the camera gives him licence to be curious, and I think that matters to him more than the photographs themselves do.

vocab.meaning: one taken without the subject posing
vocab.uz: poza bermasdan, tabiiy holda olingan surat

part2.name: Photography

practice.topic: Describe a photo that you like.
bullets: and explain why you like it
practice.answer: The photo I'd like to describe is a black-and-white picture of my grandfather, taken by my cousin at a family wedding about five years ago. My cousin is obsessed with street photography and hates posed shots, so this is a candid photo. My grandfather is caught mid-gesture, telling a story with his hands in the air, and he's laughing so hard his eyes have almost disappeared. Behind him you can see blurred guests and the edge of the dance floor. Most people would walk straight past it in an album, because it's slightly out of focus. But I love it because it shows him completely unguarded. In formal photos he always looked stiff and serious; this one strips all that away and shows the man we actually knew. It's printed and framed in our living room now, and it means even more to us than it did then. I think that picture also gave my cousin licence to photograph every family event — nobody complains about her camera anymore.

part2.topic: Describe something you do that wastes your time.
bullets: when and how often you do it
and explain why you think it wastes your time
part2.answer: The thing I'd like to talk about is my habit of scrolling through short videos on my phone, which is easily the most pointless part of my day. It happens almost entirely in the evening. I'll finish work at six, get home, tell myself I'm going to watch one or two things while dinner cooks, and then surface an hour later with no memory of anything I've seen. It also happens in bed, which is worse, because it regularly costs me forty minutes of sleep. Realistically I'd say I lose somewhere between one and two hours to it every single day. I do it because it requires absolutely nothing of me. After eight hours at a desk I don't have the energy to read properly or watch something demanding, and the app is engineered to keep you there — each video is short enough that stopping never feels like a decision you have to make. That's the clever part. You never actively choose to continue; you simply fail to stop. The reason I consider it wasted time isn't that entertainment is worthless. It's that I get nothing out of it whatsoever. I don't feel rested afterwards, I couldn't tell you a single thing I watched, and I usually feel slightly worse than when I started. Compare that with reading for an hour, which leaves me with something. I've started leaving my phone in the other room after nine, and it does help — though I'd be lying if I said I'd broken the habit.

vocab.meaning: move through content on a screen with your finger
come back to awareness after being absorbed

part2.name: A Waste of Time

practice.topic: Describe a habit you would like to change.
bullets: why you want to change it
and explain how you plan to change it
practice.answer: The habit I'd most like to change is checking my phone the moment I wake up. I think it started in my last year of school, when I began using my phone as an alarm clock. What happens is that I switch off the alarm and start to scroll through messages and news "just for a minute". Apps are designed to keep you there, and they certainly work on me — I often surface forty minutes later, still in bed and already late. I want to change it because I get nothing out of it. I don't remember what I've read, and I start the day feeling rushed and slightly anxious instead of calm. I've tried to stop several times, but I've always failed to stop after a few days, probably because I didn't replace the habit with anything else. So this time my plan is simpler. I've bought a cheap alarm clock, and my phone now charges in the kitchen overnight. People say it takes about a month to break a habit. I'm on day nine — so far, so good.

part2.topic: Describe something that you saved money for.
bullets: why you wanted to buy it
how long it took you to save the money
and explain how you felt when you finally bought it
part2.answer: The thing I saved for was a laptop — my first decent one — which I bought at the end of my second year at university. I needed it because the machine I'd inherited from my cousin was genuinely on its last legs. It took about four minutes to start up, the battery lasted twenty minutes, and it would shut down without warning, usually in the middle of something important. I'd lost an essay to it twice. Beyond the frustration, I'd started doing design work as a side job and the old laptop simply couldn't cope with the software. Saving for it took me about eight months. I was tutoring two schoolchildren in maths twice a week, and I made a rule that every som from the tutoring went straight into a separate account and was off limits. That was the part that required discipline — there were several months where I badly wanted to dip into it, particularly when friends were planning trips I couldn't afford to join. I also cut back on eating out, which saved more than I'd expected. When I finally bought it, the feeling was much stronger than I anticipated. I'd assumed I'd simply be relieved, but it was closer to pride. I think that's because I'd earned every part of it myself rather than asking my parents, which at twenty felt significant. I still have it four years later, and I've looked after it far better than I would have done if it had been handed to me.

practice.topic: Describe an expensive item you would like to buy in the future.

practice.answer: I'd really like to buy a good laptop, something powerful enough for video editing. At the moment I'm using one that was handed to me by my older brother five years ago, and it's genuinely on its last legs — the battery lasts forty minutes and the fan sounds like a helicopter. I want a new one partly for my studies, but mostly because I've started making short videos for a small online business, and my current machine simply can't cope with editing software. My plan is to save for about eight months. I've opened a separate account and told myself it's off limits, even if something tempting comes up. I've already started to cut back on taxis and eating out, which is harder than it sounds. The biggest risk is that I'll need to dip into it for an emergency. If I manage it, I'll feel really proud, because it'll be the first expensive thing I've paid for entirely by myself. And I'll definitely look after it far better than the old one.

part2.topic: Describe a good service that you received.
bullets: and explain why you thought it was good
part2.answer: The service I'd like to describe was a repair — my washing machine broke down last March and the company that fixed it went well beyond what I was expecting. It happened at home, obviously. The machine had started leaking overnight and I woke up to a flooded kitchen floor, which is not a pleasant way to begin a Tuesday. I found the company through a neighbour rather than online, which I mention because I think personal recommendations still count for a great deal here. The man who came was in his fifties and had been repairing machines for about twenty years. What impressed me first was simply that he arrived when he said he would, within the hour, which in my experience is far from guaranteed. He found the fault in about ten minutes — a perished seal — and had the part with him in the van. What made it genuinely good service, though, was everything around the repair itself. He put down a sheet before he started so he wasn't traipsing water through the flat. He showed me what had gone wrong and explained, without any talking down to me, how to spot it earlier next time. And when I asked whether the machine was worth keeping, he told me honestly that it had another four or five years in it — even though telling me to replace it would have earned him a great deal more. That last part is why I've recommended him to about six people since.

part2.name: Good Service

practice.topic: Describe a time when someone repaired something for you.
bullets: and explain how you felt about the service
practice.answer: Last winter our washing machine started leaking, so we called a repairman called Botir, who a neighbour had recommended. The problem turned out to be a perished seal on the door — a small rubber ring that had cracked with age. He explained this very patiently and never talked down to my mum, which some repairmen definitely do. Instead, he showed her exactly where the water had been escaping. What impressed me was that he went well beyond the job itself. He noticed that we'd been traipsing water through the hallway every time we emptied the machine, so he fitted a small drain pipe as well and only charged us for the parts. He even took his shoes off without being asked, which in our house counts for a great deal. I felt genuinely grateful, because honest service like that is far from guaranteed. We've had people overcharge us or disappear halfway through a job. Now Botir is the first person we call, and we've recommended him to half the building.

part2.topic: Describe a course that impressed you.
bullets: and explain why it impressed you
part2.answer: The course I'd like to describe was an introduction to graphic design that I took online about eighteen months ago, largely on a whim. It covered the fundamentals — typography, colour theory, layout, that sort of thing — and it ran for twelve weeks with a project due every fortnight. I took it entirely from home, in the evenings after work, which meant I was often opening the material at ten at night with a cup of tea. The tutor was a designer based in Berlin, and the group was scattered across about fifteen countries, so the discussions took place on a forum rather than live. What I learned was far more than I'd expected. I'd assumed it would be a matter of picking up a few software skills, but almost none of it was about software. It was about why some layouts feel calm and others feel chaotic, and how much of that comes down to spacing rather than decoration. I now find I can't look at a poster or a menu without mentally rearranging it, which is either a gift or a curse. The reason it impressed me was the quality of the feedback. Every fortnight the tutor recorded a ten- minute video going through our work individually — not written comments, but him actually talking you through what wasn't working and why. For a course that cost very little, that was an extraordinary amount of effort. It completely changed what I expect from online learning, which until then I'd rather written off.

vocab.meaning: explain it to them step by step

part2.name: Impressive Course

practice.topic: Describe something new you learned recently.
bullets: where and how you learned it
and explain how you feel about learning it
practice.answer: Recently I learned to play chess properly — not just how the pieces move, but real strategy. I signed up for a weekend course on a whim after watching a chess series online. The classes took place in a community centre near my house, every Saturday morning for two months. There were about twelve of us, from teenagers to a retired engineer. Our coach, Dilnoza, was brilliant. After every game she would talk us through our mistakes move by move, which was far more useful than simply playing. She taught us to mentally rearrange the pieces and picture the board three or four moves ahead. That took an extraordinary amount of effort at first — my head actually hurt after the early sessions. I'd always written myself off as someone who's bad at strategy games, so I'm really pleased with how it went. I'm still an average player, but I picked up enough to beat my father for the first time, which he's still not happy about.

part2.topic: Describe a skill that you learned in childhood.
bullets: when and how you learned it
and explain how useful it has been
part2.answer: The skill I want to talk about is baking bread, which I learned when I was about nine and which has stayed with me ever since. I learned it during the summers I spent at my grandmother's house in the village. There was no question of being taught formally — I simply got in her way in the kitchen often enough that she started giving me jobs. At first it was just weighing flour, then shaping the dough, and eventually she let me handle the whole thing. She baked in a tandir in the yard, so I also learned to judge when the walls were hot enough, which is entirely a matter of feel rather than temperature. My grandmother taught me, though I'd say "taught" overstates how structured it was. She never explained anything in words. She'd show me once, watch me do it wrong, and adjust my hands without saying much. Looking back, I think that's why it stuck — I learned it in my fingers rather than in my head. It's been useful in ways I never anticipated. The obvious one is that I bake most weekends and it's cheaper and better than anything I could buy. Less obviously, it's become the thing I do when I'm anxious; there's something about kneading dough that settles you down. And it's given me a way of keeping her memory alive — she passed away six years ago, and I still use her proportions, which she never once wrote down.

something judged by instinct, not measurement

part2.name: Skill

practice.topic: Describe something you learned from an older family member.
bullets: and explain why it is important to you
practice.answer: I want to talk about baking non, our traditional round bread, which I learned from my grandmother when I was about twelve. She baked every Friday in a clay tandir in the yard, and for years I just watched, because I was told I'd get in her way. Then one summer she finally let me help. She never used measurements — she said making dough was a matter of feel, and she'd make me knead it again and again until I knew when it was right. I can't overstate how patient she was. When I burned my first batch and got upset, she would settle me down with a joke and simply start again. I think that's why the lessons stuck — there was never any pressure. It's important to me because she passed away a few years ago, and baking is one way to keep her memory alive. Every time I press the pattern into the middle of the dough with her old wooden stamp, I think of her.

part2.topic: Describe a gift that you want to buy for your friend.
bullets: what you want to buy for them
and explain why you think they would like it
part2.answer: The friend I have in mind is Aziz, who I've known since we were at school together and who is about to move abroad for a two-year master's programme. What I'd like to buy him is a good fountain pen — nothing extravagant, but something properly made that will last. I've had my eye on a particular one for a few weeks now, and I'd have his initials engraved on it, which is the part that would take some organising. I chose it for two reasons. The first is practical: he's going to be writing constantly for the next two years, and he's the sort of person who still takes notes by hand because he says he remembers things better that way. The second is that he's moving three thousand kilometres away, and I wanted to give him something he'd use every single day rather than an ornament that would sit on a shelf. A pen goes in a pocket. It travels with you. I'm fairly confident he'd like it because he's always been particular about his stationery in a way the rest of us used to tease him about. He notices that sort of thing. But honestly, the object matters less than what it signals. Buying somebody a pen for a degree they're about to start is a way of saying you expect them to see it through, and I think that's the message I'd actually be sending.

have words cut into a hard surface

part2.name: Gift

practice.topic: Describe a gift you gave someone that they really liked.
bullets: and explain how the person reacted
practice.answer: Last year I gave my father a fountain pen for his sixtieth birthday. I'd had my eye on a particular one for months — a dark green pen made by a small workshop in Italy. I chose it because he's a lawyer and he's very particular about what he writes with. He still signs everything by hand and complains that cheap pens ruin his signature. I also had his initials engraved on the side, so it felt personal rather than just expensive. Getting it took some organising, since the shop didn't deliver to Uzbekistan. In the end a friend who was studying in Milan bought it and brought it back in her suitcase. There were moments when I nearly gave up and bought something local, but I'm glad I saw it through. His reaction was the best part. He's not an emotional man, but he went quiet for a moment and then used it straight away to sign my birthday card. It certainly hasn't sat on a shelf — he takes it to court every day.

part2.topic: Describe a successful business person you know.
part2.answer: The person I'd like to describe is my aunt Zulfiya, who is my mother's older sister and who has built up a textile business over the last twenty years. She started with a single sewing machine in her spare room, making school uniforms to order. She now runs a workshop employing around forty people, most of them women from her own neighbourhood, and supplies uniforms to schools across two regions. She's also branched into hotel linen, which she tells me is far less seasonal and therefore much steadier as a business. I think there are three reasons she's succeeded. The first is that she is relentlessly practical. She doesn't chase every opportunity that comes along — I've watched her turn down offers that looked lucrative because she couldn't see how she'd deliver them properly. The second is that she treats her staff extremely well. Her turnover is almost nothing, which in that industry is remarkable, and it means her quality never slips. She pays on time, every time, which sounds basic but apparently isn't. The third reason is simply that she reinvested for years when she could have taken the money out. She drove the same car for a decade while putting everything back into machinery. What I admire most, though, is that she never talks about any of it. If you met her you'd have no idea. She'd ask about your studies and say nothing about the forty people depending on her.

put profits back into the business

practice.topic: Describe a small business you know that is doing well.
bullets: and explain how you feel about it
practice.answer: I'd like to talk about a family bakery in my neighbourhood run by a woman called Malika. She built it up from a single oven in her garage about ten years ago, and now it has two shops and a delivery service. It started with traditional bread only, but a few years ago she decided to branch into cakes and pastries, which turned out to be far more profitable. Most of her orders now come from weddings and birthdays. I think she's successful for two reasons. First, she's relentlessly practical. Rather than chasing every opportunity, she only adds products she can make well, so the quality has never slipped. Second, instead of spending her profits on a big car, she reinvests almost everything in new equipment and training. I really admire her. She employs about fifteen local people, and several families depend on her business. She shows that you don't need a huge investment to succeed — just patience and good judgement.

part2.topic: Describe a person you met and want to know more about.
bullets: where and when you met them
and explain why you would like to know more about them
part2.answer: The person I'd like to talk about is a woman I met on a train last spring, whose name I only know as Malika. We were on the overnight service from Tashkent to Nukus, sharing a compartment, and we got talking somewhere around midnight because neither of us could sleep. That conversation went on for about three hours, which is not something I'd normally do with a stranger. What I know about her is quite specific but very incomplete. She's an archaeologist in her fifties, and she was travelling out to a site near the Aral Sea where she'd been working every summer for eleven years. She told me they were excavating a settlement that had been abandoned when the water receded, and that they were finding objects which suggested people had stayed far longer than anyone had assumed. She also mentioned, almost in passing, that she'd spent three years in Moscow and had walked away from a much better-paid job to do this. The reason I'd like to know more is that she described her work in a way I've rarely heard anybody describe a job. There was no complaining and no showing off — she simply talked about it as though it were the obvious thing to spend your life on. I remember thinking that I'd like to feel that way about something. We didn't exchange numbers, which I regret. I've looked her up once or twice since, without much luck.
part2.name: Interesting Person

practice.topic: Describe an interesting conversation you had with a stranger.
bullets: and explain why the conversation was interesting
practice.answer: Two years ago I travelled to Moynaq, the town that used to be a port on the Aral Sea. While I was looking at the rusting ships in the sand, I got talking to an older man selling postcards. He told me he'd been a fisherman there in the seventies, before the water receded more than a hundred kilometres. Almost in passing, he mentioned that he'd once been offered a good job in Tashkent but had walked away from it, because he couldn't imagine leaving the town where he grew up. What made the conversation so interesting was that he never tried to show off or make his story dramatic. He described the collapse of an entire industry as calmly as if he were talking about the weather. For him, staying was simply the obvious thing to do. I've thought about him a lot since then. I even tried to find him on a second visit, without much luck, which I regret, because I'd love to hear more of his stories.

part2.topic: Describe a city you've been to and you want to visit again.
part2.answer: The city I'd like to describe is Istanbul, which I visited for six days in the autumn of 2023 with two university friends. We went in late October, which turned out to be perfect timing — warm enough to walk all day but well past the summer crowds. It was my first time outside Central Asia, so almost everything about it was new to me. We did the obvious things, of course: the Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, a boat down the Bosphorus. But what I remember far more vividly is the walking. We'd pick a direction in the morning and simply set off, and we'd end up in neighbourhoods that weren't in any guidebook — steep residential streets with washing strung between the buildings and cats absolutely everywhere. We ate almost entirely at places we stumbled across. One evening we spent four hours in a tea garden above Karaköy because we couldn't bring ourselves to leave the view. What I liked most was how many things the city seemed to be at once. You'd walk ten minutes and the architecture, the language on the shop signs and the atmosphere would all shift. It felt like several cities layered on top of each other, which I found genuinely exciting rather than confusing. I want to go back because six days barely scratched the surface. There's an entire Asian side we didn't reach at all. Next time I'd go alone and stay for a fortnight.

practice.topic: Describe a trip you would like to go on again.
bullets: and explain why you would like to go again
practice.answer: I'd love to repeat a trip I took to Istanbul with two university friends the summer before last. We went in early June, which was perfect timing, because it was warm but not yet unbearably hot. We set off each morning with no fixed plan, and that turned out to be the best approach. On the second day we stumbled across a tiny bookshop tucked behind a mosque, and the owner made us tea and chatted for an hour. What fascinated me was the way different eras are layered on top of each other — Byzantine walls next to Ottoman fountains next to modern cafés. We saw the famous sights, of course, but in five days we barely scratched the surface. I'd love to go back and explore the Asian side properly, and to spend a whole day on the ferries. The other reason is that it was our last trip together before my friends moved abroad. On the final evening none of us could bring ourselves to pack, so we sat by the water until nearly two in the morning.

part2.topic: Describe a noisy place you went to.
bullets: and explain how you felt about being there
part2.answer: The noisiest place I've been to recently was a wedding hall on the outskirts of the city, where I went for a colleague's wedding in June. It was one of those enormous venues that seats several hundred people, with a stage at one end and round tables filling the rest of the floor. I arrived at about seven in the evening and stayed until nearly midnight. The noise came from several directions at once, which is what made it so overwhelming. The live band was the main culprit — the speakers were turned up far past what the room could handle, so the sound was distorting badly. On top of that there were four hundred people all shouting to be heard over the music, plus a compere with a microphone who chimed in every few minutes. At one point somebody set off fireworks outside. I genuinely could not hear the person sitting next to me, and we resorted to mouthing words and gesturing. Honestly, I found it exhausting. I've got nothing against loud celebrations — that's the tradition and people were clearly enjoying themselves — but after about three hours I had a headache and my ears were ringing. I ended up spending twenty minutes outside in the car park just to give my head a rest, which felt slightly antisocial. What surprised me is that nobody else seemed remotely bothered. I suspect I'm simply less tolerant of that kind of noise than most people, which is worth knowing about yourself.

practice.topic: Describe a place where you find it hard to concentrate.
bullets: why it is hard to concentrate there
and explain what you do about it
practice.answer: The place I find hardest to concentrate in is our university canteen. It's a huge hall that can seat several hundred students, and I end up there almost every day, because it's the only place on campus to get a cheap lunch. The noise is incredible. Every table is having its own conversation, and people chime in from the next table whenever they overhear something interesting. The main culprit, though, is the sound system. The staff turn the music up so it can be heard over the chatter, which just makes everyone talk even louder. I used to try to revise there between lectures, but it was hopeless. You can't hear your friends properly, so half the time you're mouthing words and pointing at things. After an hour, your ears are ringing. These days I eat quickly and escape to the library or a quiet bench outside. I need twenty minutes of silence to give my head a rest before afternoon classes.

part2.topic: Describe a crowded place that you went to.
bullets: and explain how you felt about being in such a crowded place
part2.answer: The place I want to describe is Chorsu Bazaar in Tashkent, which I visited two days before Eid last year — which, in hindsight, was a mistake. I went in the morning, thinking that would be the quiet part of the day. It wasn't. By the time I arrived at about nine, the approach roads were already gridlocked and I ended up walking the last kilometre because the taxi simply couldn't get through. It was crowded for the obvious reason: everybody in the city was buying food for the holiday at the same time. The meat and dried fruit sections were the worst. You didn't so much walk as get carried along by the crowd, and there were points where I couldn't have changed direction if I'd wanted to. Traders were shouting over one another, porters were pushing trolleys straight through the middle of it, and every few metres somebody was trying to hand you a sample. My feelings about it were genuinely mixed. Part of me found it stressful — I'm not especially comfortable in crowds, and I spent a lot of energy just keeping an eye on my bag. But there was also something quite wonderful about the atmosphere. Everybody was in a good mood. Complete strangers were joking with each other in the queues. By the time I got out I was exhausted and my shopping had taken three hours instead of one. Even so, I'd say the atmosphere made up for it.

part2.name: Crowded Place

practice.topic: Describe a festival or public celebration you attended.
bullets: where and when it took place
and explain how you felt about it
practice.answer: I'd like to talk about the Navruz celebrations in central Tashkent, which I went to this March with my younger brother and two cousins. Navruz is our spring new year, and on the main day the parks around Amir Temur Square are packed. The streets nearby were completely gridlocked, so we left the car and walked the last two kilometres. We spent the afternoon going from stall to stall, trying sumalak — a sweet wheat dish that's cooked overnight — and watching dancers and musicians. At times it was so crowded that it was hard to get through at all, and we simply got carried along by the crowd. I had to keep an eye on my brother the whole time, because he's only eight and kept wandering off. Despite the crush, I really enjoyed it. Everyone was in a good mood, strangers were offering each other food, and the music never stopped. The atmosphere more than made up for the aching feet and the long walk home.

part2.topic: Describe a law on environmental protection.
bullets: how you first learned about it
part2.answer: The law I'd like to describe is the restriction on single-use plastic bags, which a number of countries have now introduced in one form or another. In essence, it either bans thin plastic bags outright or forces shops to charge for them rather than handing them out free. The charge sounds trivial — a matter of pennies — but the evidence from places that have done it is that usage drops by something like eighty per cent almost immediately. People simply get into the habit of carrying a bag. I first came across it properly when I was travelling in Europe about four years ago. I was in a supermarket, went to pack my shopping, and there were no bags at the till at all. I remember feeling mildly irritated and then, about ten seconds later, slightly ashamed of feeling irritated. That small moment stuck with me far more than any article would have. The beneficiaries are fairly wide-ranging. Marine life is the most obvious one, since a great deal of this plastic ends up in rivers and eventually the sea. But municipalities benefit too, because plastic bags block drains and cause flooding, which is expensive to deal with. And ultimately the public benefits from cleaner streets. I'm strongly in favour of it. What I find persuasive is that the cost to any individual is almost nothing, while the collective effect is enormous. It's a rare example of a law that achieves a great deal by asking very little.
part2.name: Environmental Law

practice.topic: Describe a rule at your school, university or workplace that you agreed with.
bullets: and explain why you agreed with it
practice.answer: The rule I'd like to talk about was introduced at my university two years ago: the canteen stopped using disposable plastic cups and bottles. Instead of phasing them out gradually, the university banned them outright over the summer break. To make it easier, the student union handed out free reusable bottles in the first week of term, and water fountains were installed in every building. At first plenty of students complained, especially people who bought coffee between lectures. But within a couple of months most of us had got into the habit of carrying our own cups, and complaints died down. I was strongly in favour of it from the start. Before the ban, the bins overflowed every afternoon, and most of that plastic would have ended up in landfill, because the city doesn't deal with recycling well yet. It's a small change, but it's one that has stuck with me — I still carry my bottle everywhere.

part2.topic: Describe a special day out that didn't cost you a lot.
part2.answer: The day I'd like to describe was a walk in the Chimgan mountains last September, which cost the four of us almost nothing beyond the shared taxi fare. We left the city at about six in the morning, which meant we were on the trail before the heat set in. We walked for roughly five hours, stopping for a long lunch by a stream about halfway up. Everybody had brought something — bread, tomatoes, cheese, a flask of tea — so we pooled it all and ate sitting on the rocks. In the afternoon we went a little higher, to a ridge where you can see right across the valley, and then walked back down slowly. I was with three friends from university, two of whom I hadn't seen properly in over a year because we'd all drifted into different jobs in different parts of the city. What made it special wasn't the scenery, although that was extraordinary. It was that we had nothing else to do and nowhere to be. There was no bill arriving, no music, no phones — the signal cut out about twenty minutes in, which turned out to be a blessing. We talked almost continuously for eight hours, in a way you simply don't when you meet in a café for an hour and a half. I've spent a great deal more on days that were nowhere near as good. It rather reset my sense of what an outing needs to cost.

part2.name: Day Out

practice.topic: Describe a day when your plans changed unexpectedly.
bullets: and explain how you felt about the day
practice.answer: Last autumn a group of friends and I had planned a picnic in the mountains at Chimgan. We'd pooled our money to rent a minibus, and everyone had brought food. Unfortunately, about an hour after we arrived, the rain set in, and it clearly wasn't going to stop. To make things worse, the signal cut out in the valley, so we couldn't check the forecast or look for a café nearby. In the end, our driver suggested a small guesthouse a few kilometres down the road. The owner let us use a covered veranda and made us green tea, and we laid out all our food on one long table. The conversation drifted into old school stories, and before we knew it, we'd been there for five hours. The view was nowhere near as good as the one we'd planned, of course, but honestly, the rain was a blessing. With no phones and no plan, we actually talked to each other properly. Several of us still say it was the best day out we've had together.

part2.topic: Describe a time when you organized a happy event successfully.
part2.answer: The event I organised was a surprise sixtieth birthday party for my mother, which we held last autumn. It took place at my uncle's house rather than ours, for the simple reason that my mother would have noticed the preparations at home immediately. He has a large courtyard, and we set up long tables outside with lights strung between the trees. We invited about thirty-five people, mostly family, along with a handful of women she'd worked with for twenty years and hadn't seen since she retired. Organising it took roughly six weeks and the hardest part by far was keeping a lid on it. I created a group chat with everybody except her, which meant thirty-five people had to remember not to mention it, and I was genuinely amazed that nobody let it slip. I handled the food with my sister — we cooked most of it ourselves and only brought in a caterer for the plov. My cousin took care of the music. The trickiest piece of logistics was getting my mother to the house at the right time, so my father invented an elaborate story about collecting something from my uncle. It went far better than I'd expected. She worked out something was happening about ninety seconds before she walked in, which honestly made it better — she was already laughing. Several of her old colleagues stayed until well past midnight. What pleased me most was that she talked about it for weeks afterwards. That felt like the real measure of whether it had worked.
part2.name: Happy Event

practice.topic: Describe a time when someone organised a surprise for you.
practice.answer: The surprise I'll never forget was for my eighteenth birthday, and it was organised by my older sister, Nigora. I'd assumed we were just having dinner at home, but when I walked in, about thirty friends and relatives jumped out from behind the furniture. She'd even brought in a musician my dad knows, who played my favourite songs on the dutar. What amazes me is how she kept a lid on it for over a month. She set up a secret group chat and made everyone promise not to mention it. My cousin nearly let it slip a week before, when he asked what I was wearing on Saturday, but my sister quickly changed the subject. She took care of the food and the guest list, and she worked out how to keep me out of the house all afternoon by sending me on errands. I was genuinely amazed — I actually cried a bit, which everyone still teases me about. For me, the real measure of a surprise is the effort behind it, and hers was enormous.

part2.topic: Describe a time when you got stuck in a traffic jam.
part2.answer: The worst traffic jam I've been caught in was on the main road into Tashkent from the airport, about a year and a half ago. I was coming back from a work trip and heading straight to the office, because I had a presentation at two o'clock that I'd been preparing for a fortnight. Under normal conditions the journey takes forty minutes. That afternoon it took just under three hours. The cause, as far as anyone could tell, was an accident somewhere ahead combined with roadworks that had narrowed the carriageway to a single lane. We were at a complete standstill for long stretches — not crawling, but genuinely stationary, with people getting out of their cars to see what was happening. What I did was mostly damage limitation. I rang my manager within the first twenty minutes to give her the heads-up, which turned out to be the sensible decision, because they moved the presentation to the following morning. After that I rehearsed the whole thing quietly in the back seat, which the driver must have found rather strange. I also got through most of a podcast and finally answered emails I'd been putting off for a week. Emotionally it was a curve. The first half hour was pure panic. Once the meeting was rescheduled, though, the pressure lifted entirely and it became almost restful — three hours where nobody could reach me and there was nothing whatsoever I could do. I remember thinking that I hadn't sat still that long in months.

vocab.meaning: reduce the width of the road
action to reduce the harm of a problem

part2.name: Traffic Jam

practice.topic: Describe a time when you were late for something important.
bullets: and explain how you felt about it
practice.answer: The time I remember most clearly was my IELTS speaking test last year. My appointment was at nine, and I left home with what I thought was plenty of time. Unfortunately, I got caught in traffic on the ring road. Road works had narrowed the carriageway to one lane, and for about twenty minutes we were at a complete standstill. I could see the minutes ticking away on the dashboard. At that point it became a case of damage limitation. I called the test centre to give them the heads-up, and luckily the receptionist said they could move me to a later slot if I arrived by ten. I tried to calm down by listening to an English podcast — I got through two episodes before the traffic finally moved — which at least put me in the right frame of mind. I felt awful for most of the journey, but once I arrived and the examiner smiled, the pressure lifted almost immediately. In the end I got a 7.5, so maybe the podcast helped!

part2.topic: Describe a long-term goal you would like to achieve.
bullets: how you set this goal in the first place
part2.answer: The goal I'd like to describe is opening a small bookshop — one with a café attached — within the next ten years or so. The idea is deliberately modest. I'm not imagining a chain. What I have in mind is a single room with perhaps three thousand carefully chosen titles, somewhere people can sit for two hours over one coffee without anybody hurrying them along. I'd want it to host readings in the evenings. Achieving it breaks down into three things. The first is capital, and I've been putting aside a fixed proportion of my salary every month for about two years now, which will take at least another six or seven years to reach a sensible figure. The second is experience: I know nothing about retail, so I intend to spend a year working in somebody else's bookshop before I risk my own money. The third is finding the right location, which is probably the part that will make or break it. As for where the goal came from, it wasn't a single moment of inspiration. It grew out of the fact that the bookshop I used to go to as a teenager closed down about five years ago, and nothing replaced it. I found I minded far more than I expected to. I'm aware that a great many people say things like this and never act on them. What makes me think I might is that I've already started the boring part, which is usually where these plans fall down.

vocab.meaning: determine whether it succeeds or fails

vocab.uz: puchga chiqmoq, ish shu yerda to'xtaydi

part2.name: Long-Term Goal

practice.topic: Describe a goal you achieved that took a long time.
bullets: and explain how you felt when you achieved it
practice.answer: The goal I'm proudest of is running a half marathon, which I finally did last October after about eighteen months of preparation. It didn't come from a single moment of inspiration. I'd been unfit for years, and after my doctor made a comment about my fitness, I decided to act on it before it became a real problem. The key was to break it down into small stages: running for ten minutes without stopping, then five kilometres, then ten. I also put aside a little money every month for proper shoes and race fees, which made it feel like a real commitment. There were times when the whole plan nearly fell down, especially last winter, when I injured my knee and couldn't train for six weeks. My coach refused to hurry me along, and that patience probably saved the whole project. Crossing the finish line was incredible — I was exhausted but ridiculously happy. Looking back, the first three months were what made or broke it. Once running became a habit, the rest followed.

part2.topic: Describe a person who faced a big challenge but succeeded.
part2.answer: The person I want to describe is my former neighbour, Sardor, who was in his early thirties when I knew him well. The challenge he faced was that the factory he'd worked at since leaving school closed with very little warning, and he found himself out of work at thirty-two with two young children and no qualifications beyond a school certificate. In our neighbourhood at that time there was very little else going. What he did was, I think, unusually clear-headed. Rather than taking the first job available, he worked nights as a security guard — which he hated — specifically because it left his days free, and he used those days to train as an electrician. It took him about two years. He was running on very little sleep for the whole of that period, and I remember his wife saying she barely saw him. He also had to swallow his pride and borrow money from her family for the course fees, which for him was the hardest part of the whole thing. He now runs his own small electrical business and employs two people. He's considerably better off than he was before the factory closed. How I feel about it is, honestly, a mixture of admiration and slight shame. Admiration for obvious reasons. Shame because at the time I remember thinking privately that he was being unrealistic, and I said nothing to encourage him. He was right and I was wrong, and it taught me to keep that sort of judgement to myself.

vocab.meaning: accept humiliation in order to act
in a much better financial position
not say what you are thinking

part2.name: Challenge

practice.topic: Describe a person you know who changed their career.
bullets: and explain how you feel about their decision
practice.answer: I'd like to talk about my uncle Rustam, who changed career in his forties. For almost twenty years he was an engineer at a textile factory, until it closed during a restructuring and he suddenly found himself out of work. For several months he kept it to himself — he was too embarrassed to tell even his brothers. When he finally did, he had to swallow his pride and take a job as a delivery driver while he retrained in the evenings as a software tester. That period was really tough. He was running on very little sleep, working all day and studying at night. But he stayed remarkably clear-headed. He gave himself a deadline of one year, and he met it. Now he works for an IT company and is considerably better off than he ever was at the factory. I really admire him, because most people his age would have given up. I think of his story whenever I feel it's too late to change something in my own life.

part2.topic: Describe a technical problem you faced.
part2.answer: The technical problem I'd like to describe happened during my final year at university, when my laptop failed the night before a dissertation deadline. I'd been working on the document all evening. At about eleven o'clock the screen froze, and when I restarted the machine it wouldn't boot up at all — it just cycled through the manufacturer's logo over and over. The dissertation was due at nine the following morning, and while I had a version backed up, it was nearly a fortnight old and nowhere near the final draft. I'd like to say I stayed calm. In fact I spent about twenty minutes in genuine panic before I got a grip and started working through it methodically. I looked up the symptoms on my phone and found it was likely a corrupted system file rather than a hardware failure, which meant the data itself was probably intact. The solution came in two stages. First I borrowed a friend's laptop and made a bootable USB drive — something I'd never done before and which took two attempts. That let me start the machine in a recovery mode and pull the files off onto an external drive. Then I finished the last two sections on the borrowed laptop and submitted it at about seven in the morning, having pulled an all-nighter. The real lesson wasn't technical. It was that I'd been backing up manually and therefore sporadically. I've used automatic cloud backup ever since, and I've never had that particular cold sweat again.
part2.name: Technical Problem

practice.topic: Describe a time when you lost something important.
bullets: what you did to find it
practice.answer: The thing I remember losing was a USB stick containing my entire final-year project, just two days before I had to present it. I'd plugged it into a computer in the university library and walked off without it. I only realised that evening, and I broke into a cold sweat, because I'd been foolish enough not to keep a backup. I was nowhere near finished, and rewriting it would have taken weeks. After ten minutes of panicking, I told myself to get a grip. I rushed back to the library, but it was closed, so I spent the night rebuilding what I could from old emails — basically pulling an all-nighter. The next morning, the librarian had it at the front desk. My hands were shaking while the laptop booted up, but the files were all intact. I immediately pulled the files off it and saved them in three different places. I felt enormously relieved, and slightly stupid — and now I back everything up automatically.

part2.topic: Describe a person who helped you solve a problem.
part2.answer: The person I'd like to describe is a colleague of mine called Nodira, who helped me out of a difficult situation at work about eight months ago. The problem was that I had committed to a deadline I couldn't possibly meet. I'd agreed to deliver a full market report in three weeks, having badly underestimated how long the data collection would take, and by the end of the second week it was obvious I was going to fall well short. My instinct, which was the wrong one, was to say nothing and work progressively longer hours. Nodira noticed. She's about ten years older than me and she'd clearly seen this before. What she did wasn't primarily technical — although she did take two sections of the analysis off my hands. The more important thing was that she sat me down and told me, quite bluntly, that I had to tell our manager immediately rather than at the eleventh hour. She then helped me draft the message, which mattered more than I'd expected, because left to myself I would have written something defensive and apologetic rather than clear. The outcome was almost anticlimactic. Our manager moved the deadline by ten days without any real fuss and said she'd rather be told early. The report was better for the extra time. What I took from it was less about project management than about the instinct to hide bad news. Nodira's real contribution was talking me out of that, and it's changed how I handle problems since.

vocab.meaning: think something will take less time or effort than it does
fail to reach a required standard
something off someone's hands relieve them of a task
reacting as though you are being attacked
