part2.name: Problem-Solving

practice.topic: Describe a time when you gave someone good advice.
practice.answer: Last year my best friend Aziz asked for my advice when he was about to drop out of his master's programme. He'd underestimated how demanding the course would be, and after failing one exam and falling short in another, he'd decided it wasn't for him. When I first questioned his decision, he got quite defensive, so I stopped arguing and just listened. It turned out the real problem wasn't the course itself but the fact that he was also working full-time in his family's shop. So my advice was to cut his hours rather than quit his degree. I even offered to help his brother with the shop's accounts to take some of the work off his hands. In the end I managed to talk him out of leaving — at the eleventh hour, actually, because he'd already filled in the withdrawal form. He graduated this summer with a good grade, and he still jokes that he owes me a very expensive dinner. I haven't let him forget it!

part2.topic: Describe a time when you changed your opinion.
bullets: and explain how you felt afterwards
part2.answer: The opinion I changed was about learning foreign languages as an adult — specifically, I used to believe firmly that if you hadn't started young, you'd never get anywhere. I held that view for years, and I'd say it fairly confidently. My reasoning was partly anecdotal — I'd watched several adults in my family attempt English and give up — and partly that I'd absorbed the idea of a "critical period" from somewhere without ever looking into it properly. What changed my mind was my aunt, who started learning Russian at fifty-four after she retired. I was quietly sceptical, though I had the sense not to say so. Four years later she was reading novels in it and having long telephone conversations with a friend in Moscow. That undermined my position rather comprehensively. It also pushed me to read about it properly, which I should have done in the first place. It turns out the research is far more nuanced than I'd assumed: children have real advantages in pronunciation, but adults often acquire vocabulary and grammar faster because they can draw on what they already know. Where adults lose out is usually time and consistency, not capacity. Afterwards I felt two things. Slightly embarrassed, because I'd been stating something as fact that I'd never actually checked. But mostly relieved — I was twenty-eight at the time and had been quietly assuming that a door was already closed to me. Discovering it wasn't was genuinely liberating, and I started French the following year.

vocab.meaning: based on personal stories rather than evidence

part2.name: Opinion Change

practice.topic: Describe an article or book that made you think differently.
bullets: and explain how it changed your thinking
practice.answer: I'd like to talk about an article I read last year about sugar and children's behaviour. Like most people I know, I'd always believed that sugar makes kids hyperactive. The article was written by a paediatrician, and she explained that the evidence for this is mostly anecdotal. Parents see children running around at birthday parties and blame the cake, when really it's the excitement of the party. She drew on several controlled studies in which neither parents nor children knew who'd been given sugar, and there was no difference in behaviour. At first I was quietly sceptical, so I decided to look into it properly. Everything I found supported her argument, which rather undermined the position I'd defended in countless family debates. It changed my thinking in a broader way, too. The article was very nuanced — it didn't claim sugar was harmless, only that this particular belief wasn't true. Admitting I'd been wrong was surprisingly liberating, and now I try to check things before I repeat them.

part2.topic: Describe a person who has moved to a new accommodation.
part2.answer: The person I'd like to talk about is my older brother, Jasur, who moved into his first flat of his own about four months ago. He moved from our family home into a one-bedroom flat on the eighth floor of a fairly new block on the eastern side of the city. It's small — about forty square metres — and it was unfurnished, so he's spent most of the last few months slowly kitting it out. The main selling point was the location: it's a fifteen- minute walk from his office, whereas before he was commuting for over an hour each way. He moved for a combination of reasons. The commute was the practical one, and it was genuinely wearing him down — three hours a day on buses adds up. But I think the real reason was that he's thirty- one and wanted his own space. There's nothing unusual about living with your parents at that age here, and there was no falling-out whatsoever; he simply felt it was time. As for how he feels, I'd say overwhelmingly positive, with the odd wobble. He's said several times that getting those three hours back has changed his life. He cooks now, which he never did. The one thing he admits to is that the flat is very quiet in the evenings, and he hadn't bargained for how much he'd notice that. He's settling in though. My mother visits weekly with food, which I suspect suits them both.

vocab.meaning: equip it with what it needs
an argument that damages a relationship
get used to a new place

part2.name: Relocation

practice.topic: Describe a time when you moved to a new home.
bullets: what the new place was like
and explain how you felt about the move
practice.answer: Two years ago I moved out of my parents' home and into a small flat near my university. The main reason was the commute. It took almost ninety minutes each way on two buses, and it gradually wore me down. There was also a minor falling-out with my father about how late I was getting home, so we both agreed some independence would do us good. The flat was unfurnished, which I hadn't bargained for. I had to kit it out from scratch, mostly with second-hand furniture from online marketplaces, and it used up most of my savings. The main selling point was the location — it's a ten-minute walk from campus, with a small balcony that looks towards the mountains on clear days. It took me a couple of months to settle in. At first I felt quite lonely and missed my mum's cooking. But now I love having my own space, and my relationship with my parents is actually better, because we appreciate the time we spend together.

part2.topic: Describe a person who you spend most of your time with.
bullets: why you often spend time with him/her
part2.answer: The person I spend by far the most time with is my flatmate Kamola, who I've now lived with for three years. We met through a mutual friend when we were both looking for somewhere, which is a fairly hit-and-miss way of choosing who to live with, but in our case it worked out remarkably well. She's a nurse, so our schedules are completely different, and yet we still seem to overlap constantly. What we actually do together is mostly unremarkable, which I think is the point. We cook — properly, not just heating things up — usually on Sundays, and we'll make enough for the week. We watch a series together in the evenings when she's not on a night shift, and we're currently working our way through a long Turkish drama that neither of us would admit to enjoying as much as we do. Once a month or so we'll go out somewhere, but honestly the majority of our time is spent sitting at the kitchen table talking. I spend so much time with her partly through simple proximity — she's there — but that isn't really the reason. It's that she's very easy to be around. She doesn't take offence easily, she says what she thinks without any edge to it, and she's completely comfortable with silence, which I've come to value enormously. I'm aware that living arrangements change and this won't last forever. That makes me appreciate it more rather than less.

vocab.meaning: unreliable, sometimes working and sometimes not

part2.name: Spending Time

practice.topic: Describe a friend you have known for a long time.
bullets: and explain why you have stayed friends
practice.answer: I'd like to talk about my friend Kamola, who I've known since we were seven. Our first meeting was pretty unremarkable: our families lived in the same building, and proximity did the rest — we were always in each other's flats. These days we meet about once a week. We have a tradition of trying new restaurants, which is quite hit-and-miss — for every great find there's a disaster. We're also slowly working our way through a list of classic films, and we argue about every single one. I think we've stayed friends because we're completely honest with each other. She'll tell me when I'm being unreasonable, and I never take offence, because I know she means well. We also spent a year apart when she studied in Korea, and oddly, it worked out well — it made us appreciate our friendship more. She's one of those people who makes ordinary things fun, and I can't imagine life without her around.

part2.topic: Describe a time when you received something for free.
part2.answer: The thing I'd like to describe is a bicycle, which I was given for nothing about three years ago and which I still ride almost every day. It came from an elderly man who lived two doors down from my parents. He'd had it for decades — it's a heavy steel-framed thing, the sort they simply don't make now — and he'd stopped riding it some years earlier for health reasons. It had been sitting in his garage gathering dust. He knew I'd been talking about buying one because I'd asked his advice about where to look. One Saturday he knocked on the door and said he'd rather it went to somebody who'd use it than be sold to a stranger. He'd cleaned it, oiled the chain and put new tyres on it at his own expense, which I only found out about later from his wife. He refused to take a single som. How I felt was genuinely complicated. My first reaction was that I couldn't possibly accept it, and I tried to press money on him twice, which he was quite firm about refusing. Then I felt slightly overwhelmed, because it was a much bigger gesture than the object itself suggested. Mostly, though, I felt a sort of obligation — in the good sense. It made me want to be the kind of person who does that for somebody else. He died the year before last, and I've never seriously considered replacing that bicycle, even though it weighs a ton.

vocab.meaning: remain unused for a long time

vocab.phrase: go to somebody who'll use it
vocab.meaning: be given to a person who will make use of it

part2.name: Free Thing

practice.topic: Describe something you gave away.
bullets: and explain how you felt about it
practice.answer: A few months ago I gave away my old keyboard — the musical kind. I'd bought it at sixteen, intending to learn the piano, but after a year of lessons it just sat gathering dust in the corner of my room. I gave it to a ten-year-old girl who lives two doors down. Her mum had mentioned that she was teaching herself songs on a phone app, and I realised the keyboard should go to somebody who'll use it. I delivered it at my own expense, since I had to book a taxi big enough to carry it. Her parents were very grateful and kept trying to press money on me, which I refused several times. Eventually they sent round a huge tray of plov instead, which I couldn't say no to. I felt slightly overwhelmed by their reaction — in the good sense. On warm evenings I can hear her practising through the open window, and that's far more satisfying than having the keyboard in my room.

questions.question: What places do tourists usually visit?
questions.answer: It tends to be the well-known historical sites — in our case Samarkand and Bukhara, which are on almost every itinerary. Beyond that, most visitors gravitate towards markets and mountain areas, because those give you a sense of ordinary life rather than just monuments. What's changed recently is that a lot of travellers deliberately seek out places that are off the beaten track.

vocab.meaning: be part of the planned route of a trip

questions.question: What are the advantages of tourism for a country's economy?
questions.answer: The most obvious benefit is foreign currency coming into the country, which matters enormously for a developing economy. It also creates a great many jobs, and crucially those are spread across the regions rather than concentrated in the capital. There's a knock-on effect as well — hotels buy from local farmers, taxis fill up at local petrol stations. So the money circulates rather than sitting in one place.

vocab.meaning: regions be distributed around the whole country

questions.question: What are the disadvantages of tourism for local people?
questions.answer: Rising prices are the main one. When an area becomes popular, rents and everyday costs go up far faster than local wages, and residents can end up priced out of their own neighbourhood. There's also the erosion of local culture — crafts start being made for tourists rather than for use, which changes them fundamentally. And in peak season, the sheer volume of people makes ordinary life genuinely harder.

questions.question: How has tourism changed over the past 10 years?
questions.answer: The biggest shift is that it's become far more independent. People used to book a package through an agency; now they piece the whole trip together themselves online. Social media has also changed where people go — a single viral photograph can turn an unknown village into a destination overnight. And budget airlines have made travel accessible to a much wider group than before.

questions.question: How might tourism change in the future?
questions.answer: I'd expect sustainability to become the dominant concern. Several cities are already capping visitor numbers, and I think that will spread as places realise they can be loved to death. Technology will play a bigger part too — virtual tours may replace some travel, particularly for museums. But I doubt anything will genuinely replace being somewhere in person.

practice.question: Should governments limit the number of tourists visiting popular places?
practice.answer: In some cases, yes. The sheer volume of visitors in peak season can damage old buildings and make daily life miserable for residents. Capping visitor numbers at the most fragile sites seems sensible, especially if tickets can be booked in advance so people can plan around it.

practice.question: Is it better to travel independently or with a tour group?
practice.answer: It depends on the traveller. Tour groups are efficient, but independent travel lets you piece together a trip that suits you and seek out places off the beaten track. For older people or first-time travellers, though, a group can remove a lot of stress.

practice.question: How does tourism affect small local businesses?
practice.answer: Mostly positively. When a new hotel opens, there's a knock-on effect: restaurants, drivers and craftspeople all benefit. The downside is that rents rise, and small traditional shops can be priced out of the centre, replaced by stalls selling identical souvenirs.

questions.question: Why do some people enjoy cooking while others do not?
questions.answer: I think it largely comes down to whether you were brought up around it. People who cooked with a parent tend to find it relaxing, whereas those who learned as adults often experience it as a chore. There's also a personality element — cooking rewards patience, and if you're impatient the whole process feels like time you'll never get back.

vocab.meaning: something grow up with it around you
a boring, unwelcome task zerikarli yumush time you'll never get back wasted, irrecoverable time

questions.question: How important are cooking skills in modern life?
questions.answer: More important than people assume, I'd say. It's partly financial — eating out or ordering in adds up extremely quickly, and cooking is by far the cheapest way to eat well. But it's also about control over what you actually consume; when somebody else cooks, you have very little idea what's in it. I'd argue it's a life skill on a par with managing money.

vocab.meaning: have food delivered to your home

questions.question: How has technology changed the way people cook?
questions.answer: The most visible change is that recipes are now at everyone's fingertips — you can watch somebody make almost any dish in three minutes, which has made people far more adventurous. Appliances have also taken the guesswork out of a lot of it. The downside is that convenience technology, particularly the microwave, has nudged people towards processed food rather than cooking from scratch.

vocab.meaning: gently push them in a direction

questions.question: Do you think cooking skills should be taught in schools?
questions.answer: Absolutely, and I'd make it compulsory rather than optional. A great many young people leave home genuinely unable to feed themselves properly, and that has long-term consequences for their health and their finances. It doesn't need to be elaborate — half a dozen cheap, balanced meals would be enough. I'd argue it's more useful day to day than several subjects that are taken as read.

vocab.meaning: required, not optional majburiy long-term consequences for lasting effects on

questions.question: Will people cook at home less in the future?
questions.answer: Probably on weekdays, yes — delivery has become so cheap and so fast that it's hard to compete with after a long day. But I don't think home cooking will disappear, because it's shifted from a necessity to a leisure activity. People increasingly cook at weekends for pleasure rather than out of obligation. So the frequency may fall while the enthusiasm actually rises.

vocab.meaning: change from one thing into another

practice.question: Who usually does the cooking in families in your country?
practice.answer: Traditionally it's been women, and in many families it still is — sometimes out of obligation rather than choice. Attitudes are shifting in the cities, though. Younger men increasingly see cooking as a life skill, and I think it should be compulsory at school for boys and girls alike.

practice.question: Is it cheaper to cook at home than to eat out?
practice.answer: Generally, yes, especially if you cook from scratch with seasonal ingredients from the bazaar. But it comes down to time. For a busy young professional, ordering in might cost more, yet it saves an hour they simply don't have.

practice.question: Why are cooking programmes so popular?
practice.answer: Because they're entertaining rather than instructional — most viewers never cook what they watch. And now that recipes are at your fingertips online, cooking has become a hobby for many people rather than simply a necessity. Watching skilled people work is relaxing in itself.

questions.question: What types of buildings are most common in your country?
questions.answer: In the cities it's overwhelmingly apartment blocks — a great many of them built in the Soviet period, which are functional but fairly plain. In rural areas you still see traditional single-storey houses built around a courtyard, which suit the climate far better. Recently there's been a surge in glass office towers in the capital, though I'd say they sit rather awkwardly alongside everything else.

questions.question: Why do people like to visit historical buildings and sites?
questions.answer: I think there's something about standing in a place where people lived centuries ago that no photograph can convey. It gives you a physical sense of scale and craftsmanship. There's also curiosity about how people actually lived — a building tells you what they valued. And for many visitors it's a way of connecting with their own heritage rather than simply sightseeing.

vocab.meaning: skill in making things by hand
inherited traditions and buildings meros, madaniy meros sightseeing visiting places as a tourist

questions.question: Is it important for a country to protect and maintain old buildings?
questions.answer: Very much so, though I'd add that maintenance matters more than protection on paper. Plenty of countries list buildings and then let them fall into disrepair, which achieves nothing. Beyond the cultural argument, there's a practical one: restored historic quarters generate serious tourism income. Once a building is demolished, though, that decision is irreversible — and that's what makes it urgent.

questions.question: Which is more important, the architecture and design of a building or its functionality?
questions.answer: Functionality, if I had to choose — a beautiful building that's uncomfortable to work in has failed at its primary job. That said, I think the two are far less separate than the question implies. Natural light, sensible layout and good ventilation are simultaneously design decisions and practical ones. The buildings people love tend to be those where the aesthetics grew out of the function.

vocab.meaning: the flow of fresh air through a building

questions.question: What will buildings be like in the future?
questions.answer: I'd expect them to be considerably greener, largely because regulation will force it — solar panels, better insulation, possibly plants built into the facades. I also think they'll become more flexible, since the pandemic showed how quickly the purpose of a space can change. Whether they'll be taller is less obvious to me; there's a growing argument that endless height creates more problems than it solves.

vocab.meaning: more and more people claim that
vocab.uz: tobora ko'proq odam shunday deb hisoblamoqda

practice.question: Should old buildings be replaced with modern ones?
practice.answer: Not automatically. Once you demolish a historic building, the loss is irreversible. But many Soviet-era blocks are functional but plain, and replacing those with better housing makes sense. The real question is whether a building has genuine value, not just age.

practice.question: Do tall buildings make a city more attractive?
practice.answer: Sometimes. A cluster of well-designed towers can look impressive, but there's been a surge in glass towers that sit awkwardly alongside traditional low-rise neighbourhoods. A tower is only attractive if it fits its surroundings, rather than just having a shiny facade.

practice.question: Who should pay to look after historical buildings?
practice.answer: Mainly the state, because heritage belongs to everyone. Ticket revenue and private sponsors can help, of course. The worst outcome is when nobody takes responsibility and buildings fall into disrepair until they're beyond saving.

questions.question: How can people improve their sleep schedule?
questions.answer: The single most effective thing is going to bed and getting up at the same time, including at weekends, because the body responds to consistency rather than total hours. Beyond that, cutting screens an hour before bed makes a real difference, since the light suppresses the hormone that makes you drowsy. And caffeine after about two in the afternoon lingers in your system far longer than most people realise.

vocab.meaning: doing something the same way every time
stay in your body for a long time

questions.question: Why do young people prefer to stay up late?
questions.answer: Partly it's biological — there's good evidence that the body clock genuinely shifts later during adolescence, so it isn't simply a matter of discipline. But I'd say the bigger factor is that late evening is the only time young people have entirely to themselves, once school, family obligations and homework are out of the way. They're effectively reclaiming a few hours.

vocab.meaning: your natural daily rhythm biologik soat adolescence the teenage years
take back something that was lost

questions.question: Do old people get up earlier than young people?
questions.answer: Generally yes, and it seems to be genuinely physiological rather than a matter of habit. As people age their sleep becomes lighter and more fragmented, so they simply wake earlier and can't easily drop off again. There's also the practical point that most older people have no schedule forcing them to stay up, whereas younger people often work late into the evening.

vocab.meaning: relating to how the body works
sleep broken into short periods uzuq-yuluq uyqu drop off fall asleep

questions.question: Is it better to study in the morning or at night?
questions.answer: It depends enormously on the individual, but the research generally favours mornings for anything demanding, because your capacity to concentrate is highest a few hours after waking. Memory consolidation is also stronger when you study and then sleep. That said, I'd rather somebody studied at midnight with full attention than at seven in the morning while half asleep.

vocab.meaning: requiring a lot of mental effort
the process of making memories permanent

questions.question: Has technology changed the way we sleep?
questions.answer: Considerably, and mostly for the worse. Phones have made it normal to be reachable at any hour, which means the day never properly ends. Screens in bed also push bedtime later almost without you noticing — you intend to look at something for five minutes and lose forty. The one positive is that sleep tracking has made people far more conscious of how badly they're sleeping.

vocab.meaning: cause it to happen at a later time

practice.question: Why do some people find it hard to wake up early?
practice.answer: Partly it's biology — some people's body clock simply runs later than others'. But lifestyle matters too. If you go to bed at a different time every night, you'll feel drowsy whenever you get up. Consistency is probably more important than the actual hour.

practice.question: Should schools and workplaces start later in the day?
practice.answer: For teenagers, I think so. Getting them up at six clearly damages their capacity to concentrate, so a nine o'clock start could improve results. For adults, flexible hours seem fairer, since some people like to get their work out of the way early.

practice.question: Why do people today get less sleep than in the past?
practice.answer: Mostly because of phones. People feel they need to be reachable at any hour, so they check messages in bed and drop off much later. Notifications during the night also cause fragmented sleep, which can be almost as bad as not sleeping enough.

questions.question: Do you think young people and older people have different attitudes towards laws?
questions.answer: I'd say the difference is more about which laws than about respect for law in general. Older people tend to view rules as legitimate by default, having grown up in a more hierarchical period, whereas younger people are more inclined to ask what a rule is actually for. That isn't disrespect so much as a different starting point — they'll comply, but they want the reasoning.

vocab.meaning: automatically, unless proved otherwise boshidanoq, aks holi isbotlanmaguncha hierarchical based on strict levels of authority

questions.question: Do you think people today are more law-abiding than in the past? Why?
questions.answer: In most respects yes, though I suspect it's less about morality than about the likelihood of getting caught. Cameras, digital payments and databases mean that a great deal of minor crime is now simply not worth attempting. Levels of violence have also fallen substantially over the long term. So I'd say people are better deterred rather than fundamentally better behaved.

vocab.meaning: not worth the risk of trying
discourage them from acting through fear of consequences

questions.question: Do you think it is okay for people to break rules in some situations?
questions.answer: In genuine emergencies, clearly yes — nobody would criticise a driver for running a red light to get somebody to hospital. Beyond that I'd be cautious, because everyone believes their own exception is reasonable. The stronger case is civil disobedience, where a law is itself unjust and breaking it openly is the only way to challenge it. But that requires accepting the consequences, which is what separates it from simply cheating.

vocab.meaning: drive through a red traffic signal
deliberately breaking an unjust law as protest
face the results of your actions

questions.question: What kinds of rules do children usually dislike?
questions.answer: Anything that feels arbitrary, in my experience. Children will accept a rule remarkably well if the reasoning is explained, but "because I said so" tends to produce resistance. They particularly resent rules about bedtime and screen time, because those directly restrict things they enjoy. Uniform rules are another one — they're the classic example of a rule children see as serving the institution rather than them.

vocab.meaning: based on nobody's reasoning, seemingly random

questions.question: Are different punishments important to prevent crime?
questions.answer: I think proportionality matters more than severity. If every offence carried the same penalty, there'd be no incentive to commit the lesser one, which is precisely why the scale exists. The evidence also suggests that the certainty of punishment deters far more effectively than its harshness — people are stopped by expecting to be caught, not by the length of the sentence. So variety is useful, but it isn't the main lever.

vocab.meaning: the principle that punishment should match the crime
have a punishment attached to it
a reason to behave in a certain way

practice.question: Why do some people break the law?
practice.answer: Often because they believe the likelihood of getting caught is low. Most people who run a red light, for instance, aren't criminals — they just assume no one is watching. Otherwise law-abiding people will cut corners if the risk seems small enough.

practice.question: Are fines the best way to stop people breaking minor laws?
practice.answer: Fines work, but only if they're enforced consistently. What really deters people is certainty, not the size of the fine. It also helps to offer an incentive for good behaviour, such as cheaper insurance for drivers with a clean record.

practice.question: Should parents set strict rules for teenagers?
practice.answer: Some rules, yes, but they need to make sense. Teenagers resent rules that feel arbitrary, and they'll simply break them in secret. If parents explain why something matters and agree in advance what carries a penalty, teenagers are far more likely to cooperate.

questions.question: What kinds of plants do people grow in your country?
questions.answer: Fruit trees above all — apricots, cherries and grapes are almost universal in courtyards, and most households grow far more than they can eat, so a great deal gets dried or preserved. Vegetables are common too, particularly tomatoes and herbs. In the cities, where space is limited, people make do with pots on balconies, usually flowers rather than anything edible.

vocab.meaning: treat it so it lasts longer
an enclosed yard beside a house

questions.question: Why do some people enjoy growing plants?
questions.answer: I think the main appeal is that it gives you a visible result over time, which very little modern work does — most jobs produce nothing you can hold. It's also genuinely calming; there's a body of research suggesting gardening lowers stress considerably. And for a lot of people there's satisfaction in self-sufficiency, however small, in eating something you grew yourself.

vocab.meaning: providing for yourself without outside help
even if it is very small

questions.question: Is growing plants more of a hobby or a duty?
questions.answer: That divides fairly sharply by generation and by place, I'd say. For my grandparents' generation in rural areas it was straightforwardly a means of putting food on the table — not something you'd describe as enjoyable. For city dwellers today it's almost entirely recreational. What's interesting is that the same activity can feel like drudgery when it's necessary and like therapy when it's optional.

questions.question: Should schools teach students how to grow plants?
questions.answer: I'd support it, mainly because a striking number of children have no idea where food actually comes from. Growing something from seed makes that concrete in a way a textbook can't. It also teaches patience, which is in short supply in a generation used to instant results. I wouldn't make it a major subject, but a school garden costs very little and teaches a great deal.

vocab.meaning: something concrete make an abstract idea real and clear

questions.question: Should governments encourage people to grow plants?
questions.answer: Encourage, certainly — though I'd focus on making it possible rather than urging people to do it. Providing allotments and community gardens in dense urban areas would achieve far more than a public awareness campaign. There are real collective benefits: greener cities are cooler in summer, and green space measurably improves mental health. So I'd see it as sound public policy rather than a lifestyle matter.

vocab.meaning: a small plot of public land rented for growing food
an official effort to inform people
parks and planted areas in a city yashil hudud sound policy sensible, well-judged policy

practice.question: Do young people in your country enjoy gardening?
practice.answer: Not many, to be honest. For their parents' generation, working the land often meant drudgery, so young people don't associate it with fun. That's slowly changing, though — growing herbs or other edible plants on a balcony has become quite trendy.

practice.question: Is it better to grow your own food or to buy it?
practice.answer: Growing your own is more satisfying, especially when you raise something from seed. But complete self-sufficiency isn't realistic for most families. In rural areas, a vegetable plot still genuinely helps put food on the table.

practice.question: Why has gardening become popular in cities?
practice.answer: Because people crave contact with nature. Most city dwellers have to make do with a balcony or a window box, while in some countries residents can rent an allotment. For them, gardening is recreational rather than economic — a way to unwind after work.

questions.question: Is it easy to make new friends today?
questions.answer: It's easier to meet people and harder to become close to them, which is a strange combination. Online you can find somebody who shares any interest within minutes. But real friendship needs repeated unplanned contact — the kind you get at school or in a shared office — and adult life provides very little of that. So people have wider networks and fewer genuine friends.

questions.question: Do you think childhood friendships usually last forever?
questions.answer: A few do, but I'd say most don't, and I don't think that's a failure. Childhood friendships are largely built on proximity — you were in the same class — rather than on choosing each other. Once people move away or take different paths, there's often very little holding it together. The ones that survive tend to be those that were rebuilt on something deeper in adulthood.

questions.question: Is it better to have many friends or just a few close ones?
questions.answer: A few close ones, without much hesitation. Friendship requires time, and time is finite — thirty friendships inevitably means thirty shallow ones. What people actually need in a crisis is two or three people they can ring at midnight. That said, a wider circle of acquaintances is genuinely useful for opportunities and perspective, so I'd say the ideal is a small core with a broad edge.

vocab.meaning: lacking depth yuzaki, sayoz an acquaintance someone you know slightly

questions.question: Why do some friendships fade away over time?
questions.answer: Usually through neglect rather than conflict. Very few friendships end in an argument; they simply stop being maintained because both people are busy and each assumes the other will get in touch. Life changes accelerate it — one marries, one moves abroad, one has children — and the common ground that held them together quietly disappears. It's rarely anybody's decision.

vocab.meaning: failure to give attention to something

questions.question: Does social media make people feel lonelier?
questions.answer: For a lot of people, yes, though I think the mechanism is often misunderstood. It isn't the contact itself that's harmful — it's the comparison. You're seeing everybody's edited highlights while living your own unedited life, which reliably makes you feel left out. Used deliberately to arrange meeting people, it does the opposite. The problem is passive scrolling, not the technology.

vocab.meaning: the act of measuring yourself against others
only the best moments, carefully selected

practice.question: What makes someone a good friend?
practice.answer: Loyalty, mainly — someone who stays around when things go wrong. Shared humour matters too. You don't need identical interests, but you do need some common ground, otherwise conversations dry up quickly.

practice.question: Is it possible to be real friends with your colleagues?
practice.answer: Definitely. Many people become close to colleagues in adulthood, simply because they spend more time with them than with anyone else. But office friendships can be fragile — when someone changes jobs, a close friend can quickly become an acquaintance.

practice.question: Can a friendship survive if friends live in different countries?
practice.answer: It can, but it takes effort. When friends take different paths, it's easy to neglect the relationship without meaning to, so it's important to get in touch regularly, even briefly. And when one friend builds a new life abroad, the other can easily feel left out.

questions.question: What kind of plans do people in your country usually make?
questions.answer: Family events dominate, I'd say — weddings in particular are planned a year or more in advance and involve an enormous amount of coordination. Financially, people tend to plan around large one-off purchases like a car or a house rather than through long-term investment. Day to day, I'd say planning is fairly loose; arrangements with friends are often made the same morning.

vocab.meaning: before the time something happens oldindan coordination organising people and tasks together

questions.question: Do you think planning ahead is important? Why?
questions.answer: Very, though mostly for a reason people don't often state: planning reduces the number of decisions you have to make under pressure. If you've thought something through in advance, you're not improvising while stressed, and stressed improvisation is where mistakes happen. It also surfaces problems early, when they're still cheap to fix. The caveat is that over-planning can become a way of avoiding starting.

vocab.uz: shu bilan birga, bir shart bor

questions.question: Why do some people dislike planning?
questions.answer: For some it's simply that plans feel constraining — they'd rather keep their options open and respond to whatever comes up. Others avoid it because planning forces you to confront what you actually want, which can be uncomfortable. And there's a practical reason too: if your circumstances are unstable, detailed plans are constantly overtaken by events, so people learn there's little point.

questions.question: How do people usually make plans in your country?
questions.answer: Almost entirely through Telegram, at this point — group chats have replaced phone calls for anything involving more than two people. For family occasions, though, the planning is still largely verbal and quite hierarchical; the older members take the lead and the rest fall in behind. Written schedules are rare outside a work context, which does mean things sometimes run late.

questions.question: Has technology changed the way people plan their lives?
questions.answer: Enormously, and I'd say in two opposite directions. Shared calendars and reminders have made detailed coordination far easier than it was. But messaging has also made plans much more provisional — because you can cancel by text in three seconds, people commit less firmly and change arrangements at the last minute far more than they used to. So planning is simultaneously more precise and less reliable.

practice.question: Are some people naturally better at planning than others?
practice.answer: I think so. Some people instinctively think things through, while others prefer to improvise and deal with problems as they arise. In a group, the planners usually take the lead, which tends to suit everyone.

practice.question: Is it wise to plan your career when you're young?
practice.answer: Up to a point. Having a direction is useful, but it's sensible to keep your options open, because industries change so fast. A rigid ten-year plan can easily be overtaken by events, as many people discovered during the pandemic.

practice.question: Should people make detailed plans for their holidays?
practice.answer: A rough plan makes sense — booking flights and the first hotel in advance saves money and stress. But I'd keep the rest provisional. Some of the best travel experiences happen when you decide at the last minute to go somewhere new.

questions.question: What types of food do people usually eat on special occasions?
questions.answer: Plov is the obvious one here — it's served at virtually every wedding, funeral and major holiday, and it's cooked in enormous quantities by men rather than women, which is unusual. Beyond that, tables at celebrations are laden with dried fruit, nuts and sweets. The pattern generally is that celebration food is labour-intensive; the effort itself is part of the gesture.

vocab.meaning: be provided as food at an event

questions.question: Do people today eat healthier than in the past?
questions.answer: It cuts both ways. People are far better informed — nutritional labelling and general awareness are vastly better than a generation ago, and there's much more variety available year-round. But the food itself has got worse: ultra-processed products now make up an enormous share of the average diet, and portion sizes have grown considerably. So knowledge has improved while behaviour arguably hasn't.

vocab.meaning: have both good and bad aspects
information about food content on packaging
how much food is served at once

questions.question: What are the effects of fast food on society?
questions.answer: The health consequences are the most discussed — rising rates of obesity and related illness place a considerable burden on health systems. But there are cultural effects too. Fast food has eroded the habit of eating together, because it's designed to be consumed alone and quickly. On the other hand it's genuinely convenient for people working long hours, so I'd be wary of demonising it entirely.

vocab.meaning: create a heavy cost or pressure for

questions.question: Why do people prefer eating out nowadays?
questions.answer: Time is the honest answer — when both partners work full-time, nobody wants to cook at eight in the evening. But it's also become a social ritual in a way it wasn't for my parents' generation; meeting friends now almost automatically means a restaurant. And restaurants have simply got better and cheaper, so the gap between eating out and cooking has narrowed considerably.

vocab.meaning: working the standard complete working week
a regular shared social activity ijtimoiy odat, an'anaviy uchrashuv narrow (of a gap) become smaller
without needing to think about it

questions.question: How might people's eating habits change in the future?
questions.answer: I'd expect meat consumption to fall, driven less by ethics than by cost and environmental regulation. Plant-based alternatives are improving quickly and will probably become the default in processed products long before people notice. I also think personalisation will grow — diets tailored to individual data. What I doubt is that traditional cooking will disappear; it's too bound up with identity for that.

vocab.meaning: made from plants rather than animals

practice.question: Is traditional food in your country healthy?
practice.answer: Partly. Dishes like plov are laden with oil and meat, so they're heavy if you eat them every day. But there are plenty of fresh salads and soups too, and home cooking avoids ultra-processed ingredients, which is a big advantage.

practice.question: Should governments try to control what people eat?
practice.answer: Only gently. Clear information about portion sizes and sugar content helps people choose, but I'd be wary of banning foods outright. Taxes on sugary drinks cut both ways — they work, but they hit poorer families hardest.

practice.question: Why is eating together important in many cultures?
practice.answer: Because meals are a social ritual, not just nutrition. Traditional dishes are often labour-intensive, so even preparing them brings people together. That's partly why people resist plant-based alternatives at celebrations — the dish carries meaning, not just flavour.

questions.question: What kinds of sports events are most popular in your country?
questions.answer: Football draws the biggest crowds by some distance, particularly national team matches, which people watch collectively in cafés even without tickets. Wrestling has enormous cultural weight too — traditional kurash competitions at holidays attract huge numbers. Boxing has grown considerably as well, largely on the back of a few internationally successful athletes.

vocab.meaning: importance within a culture madaniy ahamiyat on the back of as a result of

questions.question: What are the differences between watching sports live in a stadium and watching them on TV?
questions.answer: The obvious difference is atmosphere — in a stadium you're part of a crowd and the emotion is contagious in a way a screen simply can't reproduce. Television, though, gives you a far better view of the actual play: replays, multiple angles and commentary explaining what happened. So you understand more on television and feel more in a stadium.

vocab.meaning: a repeated showing of a moment

questions.question: Why do some people enjoy watching sports instead of playing them?
questions.answer: For many it's simply a question of ability and age — you can watch football at any standard, but playing it well requires a level most people never reach. Watching also offers something playing doesn't: a shared identity. Supporting a team gives you an instant connection with complete strangers. And there's the drama of it, which is genuinely unscripted in a way television drama isn't.

vocab.meaning: a sense of belonging to the same group
not planned or written in advance

questions.question: Do you think international sports events are beneficial for a country?
questions.answer: They can be, but the evidence is more mixed than governments suggest. The benefits are real — international visibility, improved infrastructure and a genuine sense of national pride. The problem is cost: stadiums built for a single tournament frequently become white elephants that cost money for decades. I'd say the events are worth hosting when the infrastructure was needed anyway, and rarely otherwise.

vocab.meaning: roads, transport and public facilities infratuzilma a white elephant an expensive thing that is useless to maintain

questions.question: How might sports events change in the future?
questions.answer: I'd expect the viewing experience to change more than the sports themselves. Streaming has already broken the hold traditional broadcasters had, and personalised camera angles are probably not far off. There's also growing pressure over scheduling — matches kicking off at strange hours to suit foreign markets. And climate will increasingly dictate where and when summer events can be held at all.

vocab.meaning: something end its control or dominance

practice.question: Why do people support their national teams so passionately?
practice.answer: Because sport gives people a shared identity. When the national team plays, strangers suddenly feel connected, and the excitement is contagious. Football in particular can draw a crowd of people who never normally watch sport.

practice.question: Should governments spend money on hosting big sporting events?
practice.answer: It can pay off by improving infrastructure and giving a country global visibility. But there's a real risk of building a stadium that becomes a white elephant afterwards. Countries should only host an event if the facilities will be used long after it ends.

practice.question: Is watching sport a good way to spend free time?
practice.answer: In moderation, yes. Unlike films, sport is unscripted, so it's genuinely exciting — anything can happen in the last minute. The problem is when watching completely replaces playing.

questions.question: Why are holidays important in people's lives?
questions.answer: The obvious reason is recovery — sustained work without a proper break leads fairly reliably to burnout, and a weekend isn't long enough to undo that. But I'd argue the bigger value is perspective. Stepping outside your routine tends to make it clear which parts of it you actually want to return to. Holidays also give families concentrated time together, which ordinary weeks rarely allow for.

vocab.meaning: leave room or time for it

questions.question: How do people usually spend their holidays in your country?
questions.answer: A great many people spend them with extended family rather than travelling — visiting relatives in the regions is the default for major holidays. Those who do travel tend to go to the mountains in summer, or to Turkey and Dubai if the budget stretches to a flight. What's less common here than in Europe is the idea of a holiday spent entirely alone; it's fundamentally a social occasion.

vocab.meaning: what happens automatically unless decided otherwise
be just enough to afford it
an event centred on being with others

questions.question: What are the places that people usually go to for holidays?
questions.answer: Coastal destinations dominate, which I think is partly because we're landlocked and the sea has a novelty here that it doesn't elsewhere. Domestically, Chimgan and the Fergana Valley are popular for short breaks. There's also been a marked rise in city breaks — people taking three or four days in Istanbul or Almaty rather than a fortnight anywhere, largely because it's cheaper and easier to fit around work.

vocab.meaning: something around work arrange it to suit your job

questions.question: How important is preparation before going on holiday?
questions.answer: It matters more than people expect, though I'd distinguish between logistics and itinerary. Sorting out documents, insurance and accommodation in advance genuinely saves you a great deal of grief. Planning every hour, on the other hand, tends to defeat the object — you end up managing a schedule instead of resting. The ideal is a firm framework with plenty of slack inside it.

questions.question: How have holidays changed compared to the past?
questions.answer: They've become shorter and more frequent — people now take several long weekends rather than one substantial break, largely because cheap flights make that viable. Booking has shifted almost entirely online, which has cut agencies out of the process. The less welcome change is that work has followed people onto the beach; before smartphones, being on holiday meant being genuinely unreachable, and that's largely gone.

vocab.meaning: someone out of something remove them from a process

practice.question: Is it better to take one long holiday or several short ones?
practice.answer: Several short ones suit most people. They're easier to fit around work, and they help prevent burnout, because you never go too long without a break. That said, a long trip is the only way to properly step outside your routine.

practice.question: Should employers encourage staff to switch off completely on holiday?
practice.answer: Absolutely. If people answer emails from the beach, they come back just as tired. Some companies now let employees be completely unreachable, which I think saves everyone grief in the long run — staff return rested and more productive.

practice.question: Do people in your country usually go on holiday with their families?
practice.answer: Very much so. Holidays often mean visiting extended family rather than travelling abroad. Organising the logistics for twenty relatives is a nightmare, but for many people, travelling alone is still a novelty.

questions.question: Why is decision-making important in people's lives?
questions.answer: Because the shape of a life is essentially the accumulation of its decisions — where you study, who you marry, what you turn down. Most of those can't be reversed, or can only be reversed at considerable cost. There's also the point that not deciding is itself a decision; people who postpone indefinitely usually find circumstances decide for them, and rarely in their favour.

questions.question: What about at work?
questions.answer: At work I'd say the key difference is that decisions carry consequences for other people, not just yourself, which raises the standard considerably. Speed also matters more — a good decision made late is often worth less than an adequate one made on time. And there's the question of accountability: in an organisation somebody has to own the outcome, which is precisely why many people avoid deciding at all.

vocab.meaning: take full responsibility for a result

questions.question: How can people improve their decision-making skills?
questions.answer: The most practical technique is writing down your reasoning at the time, because memory quietly rewrites it afterwards to make you look wiser than you were. Reviewing old decisions honestly is how you actually learn. Beyond that, it helps to distinguish reversible from irreversible choices and stop agonising over the reversible ones. And deliberately seeking out somebody who disagrees with you surfaces what you've missed.

questions.question: What kinds of decisions do young people today have to make?
questions.answer: The traditional ones remain — what to study, whether to move abroad, when to marry — but I'd say the pressure has intensified because the range of options has widened enormously. A generation ago most people followed a fairly prescribed path. Now young people also face decisions their parents never did, about online identity and about careers that may not exist in fifteen years.

vocab.meaning: a route laid out for you by others

questions.question: Do you think children should get advice before making important decisions?
questions.answer: Advice yes, instructions no — and I think that distinction is where a lot of parents come unstuck. Children need somebody to help them think through the consequences, because their sense of the long term is genuinely undeveloped. But if adults simply decide for them, they reach eighteen having never practised. I'd rather a child made a small mistake at twelve than a large one at twenty-five.

vocab.meaning: the distant future uzoq muddat, kelajak practise (a skill) do it repeatedly to improve

practice.question: Why do some people find it hard to make decisions?
practice.answer: Often it's fear of regret. People agonise over choices that carry consequences for years, such as which university to attend. And sometimes there are just too many options — choosing between two phones is easy, but choosing between thirty is exhausting.

practice.question: Is it better to make decisions quickly or slowly?
practice.answer: It depends on whether the decision is reversible. Small, easily changed choices should be quick. Big ones deserve time, because you can't always reverse a decision once it's made, and people who rush those usually come unstuck.

practice.question: Do young people today have more choices than their parents did?
practice.answer: Far more. Our parents often followed a prescribed path: study, marry, stay in one job for life. Now the range of options is huge, and people even turn down secure jobs to try something new, which is exciting but also stressful.

questions.question: Is it always better to work in a group?
questions.answer: Certainly not — I'd say it depends entirely on the nature of the task. Anything requiring sustained concentration, like writing or detailed analysis, is usually done better alone, because groups fragment attention. Where teams genuinely help is on problems that need several kinds of expertise, or where the work is simply too large for one person. Using a team on the wrong task just adds overhead.

vocab.meaning: deep focus over a long period
extra effort that produces no direct value

questions.question: What problems can happen when people work as a team?
questions.answer: The most common is unequal contribution — one or two people carry the work while others coast, which breeds resentment quickly. Then there's the tendency for groups to converge on a safe, mediocre answer because nobody wants to disagree openly. Communication overhead is another real cost: past a certain size, teams spend more time coordinating than producing. And diffused responsibility means mistakes often go unowned.

vocab.meaning: some people doing far more than others
do the minimum while others work
responsibility spread so thin nobody feels it

questions.question: Should schools teach children teamwork skills?
questions.answer: Yes, but properly rather than by simply assigning group projects and leaving them to it, which is what usually happens. Unstructured group work often teaches the wrong lesson — that the diligent child does everything. Real teaching would mean explicit roles, individual accountability within the group, and discussion afterwards about what went wrong. Otherwise you're just rehearsing bad habits for eleven years.

vocab.meaning: let them get on without guidance
hard-working and careful tirishqoq, mehnatkash rehearse a habit practise it until it becomes automatic

questions.question: How can people improve their teamwork skills?
questions.answer: The single most useful skill is listening properly rather than waiting for your turn to speak, which most people confuse with listening. Beyond that, being explicit about who is doing what prevents the majority of team failures before they start. Learning to disagree without it becoming personal is harder but essential. And it genuinely helps to work with people who are unlike you, because that's what stretches you.

vocab.phrase: wait for your turn to speak
vocab.meaning: listen only in order to reply
state something clearly rather than assuming

questions.question: Which is more effective: working alone or working in a team?
questions.answer: I don't think there's a general answer, but if pressed I'd say the most effective arrangement is neither — it's alternating between the two. The pattern that seems to work best is teams meeting to define the problem, individuals going away to think properly, then reconvening to combine. Continuous collaboration produces shallow work; total isolation produces work that misses the point.

vocab.meaning: if forced to give an answer
fail to address what actually matters

practice.question: What makes a good team leader?
practice.answer: Mainly the ability to assign tasks clearly and be explicit about who is responsible for what. Without that, you get diffused responsibility, where everyone assumes someone else will do the job.

practice.question: Is group work at school fair to all students?
practice.answer: Often not. There's nearly always unequal contribution: one or two students do most of the work while others coast. That can breed resentment, so teachers should assess individual input as well as the final product.

practice.question: Are some jobs better done alone?
practice.answer: Definitely. Writing, programming and research need sustained concentration, and constant meetings get in the way. A good compromise is to work alone and meet to review progress, as long as people don't take feedback personally.

questions.question: Why do some people want to start their own business?
questions.answer: Autonomy is the reason people give most often — not answering to anybody, choosing what you work on. Financial upside matters too, since employment caps what you can earn in a way ownership doesn't. But I suspect the deeper motivation for many is wanting their effort to accrue to themselves rather than to an employer. There's also a large group who start businesses simply because they couldn't find a job.

vocab.meaning: set an upper limit on it

questions.question: Do you agree that today it's easier to set up a business than in the past?
questions.answer: Easier to start, considerably harder to succeed. The barriers to entry have collapsed — you can register a company online and reach customers through social media with almost no capital. But precisely because everyone can do that, the market is far more crowded and customer attention is the scarce resource now, not capital. So the first step is easy and the tenth is harder than ever.

questions.question: Do people like to work in big companies or small ones?
questions.answer: It divides fairly predictably by what people want. Large companies offer security, structure and a clear career ladder, which suits people with dependants. Small firms offer variety and visible impact — your work obviously matters, which is motivating in a way it rarely is in a corporation. In my experience younger people gravitate towards small firms and then move to larger ones once they want stability.

vocab.meaning: family members who rely on your income
an effect you can clearly see

questions.question: What challenges do start-ups usually face?
questions.answer: Cash flow is the one that kills most of them — a business can be profitable on paper and still fail because money arrives later than it leaves. Finding customers is the second; founders consistently underestimate how long that takes. Then there's hiring, because good people are reluctant to join something unproven. And founders frequently spread themselves too thin, doing everything badly rather than one thing well.

vocab.meaning: the movement of money in and out of a business
showing profit in the accounts only
think something is smaller or easier than it is
take on too many things at once
vocab.uz: kuchini juda ko'p ishga bo'lib yubormoq

questions.question: What makes some companies more successful than others?
questions.answer: I'd put execution above the idea itself — plenty of companies have succeeded with unoriginal ideas simply by doing them well and consistently. Understanding customers properly rather than assuming is the second factor. Beyond that, the ability to adapt matters enormously; the firms that fail are often those that were right once and stopped listening. And luck plays a far larger role than successful founders tend to admit.

vocab.meaning: how well a plan is actually carried out

practice.question: What qualities does a successful entrepreneur need?
practice.answer: Resilience, first of all, and the ability to adapt. Ideas matter less than people think — execution is what separates success from failure. Plenty of people have a good idea; very few carry it through.

practice.question: Is it better to be an employee or to run your own business?
practice.answer: It depends on your personality. Running a business gives you autonomy — you don't have to answer to anybody. But employees have stability, and many people value security over freedom, which is perfectly reasonable.

practice.question: Why do so many new businesses fail?
practice.answer: Often it's cash flow: they run out of money before the profits arrive. Online, low barriers to entry mean a crowded market, so competition is fierce. Founders also tend to spread themselves too thin, trying to do everything instead of one thing well.

questions.question: Why do some people prefer living in apartments rather than houses?
questions.answer: Cost is the primary reason — a flat in a good location is usually far cheaper than a house anywhere comparable. Maintenance is the second: the building's upkeep is shared, so you're not personally responsible for the roof. Flats also tend to be central, which cuts commuting substantially. And for older people or those living alone, there's genuine value in having neighbours within earshot.

vocab.meaning: the cost and work of maintaining something

questions.question: What are the differences between traditional homes and modern homes?
questions.answer: Traditional houses here were built around a courtyard, with thick walls and small windows, which is an extremely effective response to a hot dry climate. Modern flats are the opposite — large glazed areas that then require air conditioning to be habitable. Traditional homes also assumed several generations under one roof, whereas modern layouts are designed for a nuclear family or an individual.

vocab.meaning: built around something be designed with it at the centre
fitted with glass oynali, oynavand habitable fit to live in

questions.question: What makes a home comfortable to live in?
questions.answer: Light is the thing I'd put first — a well-lit room feels larger and noticeably better to be in, and it's very difficult to compensate for its absence. Beyond that, sound insulation matters more than people realise until they don't have it. Temperature control, obviously. But I'd also say a home is comfortable when the layout matches how you actually live, rather than how the architect assumed you would.

vocab.meaning: make up for the absence of something
material that blocks noise shovqindan izolyatsiya layout how rooms are arranged

questions.question: Does the place where people live affect their mood and personality?
questions.answer: Mood, unquestionably — there's solid evidence linking natural light, noise levels and green space to mental health. Personality is a stronger claim, but I'd say environment shapes behaviour over time, and behaviour eventually hardens into character. Somebody who lives somewhere with a strong sense of community is likely to become more sociable simply through repeated interaction. So the effect is real but gradual.

vocab.meaning: strong, reliable proof ishonchli dalil harden into gradually become something fixed
the feeling that neighbours belong together

questions.question: Will smart homes become common in the future?
questions.answer: In some form, certainly, though I suspect not the way it's currently marketed. What will become standard is the invisible part — heating that manages itself, lighting that responds to occupancy — because those save money. The novelty features like talking fridges will probably fall by the wayside. The real obstacles are security and the fact that nothing talks to anything else reliably yet.

vocab.meaning: whether a room is being used

practice.question: Is it common for young people in your country to live with their parents?
practice.answer: Very common — traditionally, several generations under one roof was the norm. Many young couples still move in with the husband's parents. It's cheaper, and there's always someone within earshot to help with the children, but privacy can be limited.

practice.question: What should architects consider when designing new homes?
practice.answer: Practical things first: a sensible layout, rooms that are well-lit, and proper sound insulation in apartment blocks. They should also design shared spaces, like courtyards, that encourage a sense of community.

practice.question: Is it better to rent or to buy a home?
practice.answer: Buying is the dream here, because renting is seen as money thrown away. But owners pay for all the upkeep, while renting gives flexibility. In some countries lifelong renting has become standard, and I think attitudes here may shift too.

questions.question: What are the advantages of living in a big city?
questions.answer: Opportunity, above everything — the concentration of employers means far more chance of finding work that genuinely suits you. Services follow the same logic: specialist hospitals, universities and cultural venues only make sense at scale. There's also anonymity, which sounds negative but matters a great deal to anyone who doesn't fit the local mould. Cities are, on the whole, more tolerant places.

vocab.meaning: a large number gathered in one place
only be viable with large numbers
not being known or watched by others
conform to what is expected locally

questions.question: What are the disadvantages of living in a city?
questions.answer: Cost is the headline one — housing in particular absorbs a proportion of income that would be unthinkable elsewhere. Then there's the commuting, which for many people amounts to two hours of their day gone permanently. Air quality is a genuine health issue in most large cities. And despite being surrounded by people, urban life can be curiously isolating, because proximity isn't the same as connection.

vocab.meaning: the most obvious and important one

questions.question: How have cities changed over the past few decades?
questions.answer: They've grown enormously, mostly outwards rather than upwards, which has made car dependence far worse. Many have also seen their centres shift from residential to commercial, hollowing out neighbourhoods that were once lived in. On the positive side, a lot of cities have reclaimed space from cars — pedestrianised streets and cycle lanes were rare thirty years ago and are now fairly standard.

vocab.meaning: reliance on private cars for everything
empty it of what made it alive
take back land for a different use

questions.question: How might cities change in the future?
questions.answer: I'd expect the biggest driver to be climate — cities in hot regions will have to retrofit shade, water and greenery simply to remain liveable in summer. Remote work may also loosen the grip of the centre, spreading activity into smaller satellite towns. And I think car ownership will decline in dense areas, not because of policy so much as because it will become more trouble than it's worth.

vocab.meaning: the main cause of it harakatlantiruvchi kuch retrofit add something to an existing structure

questions.question: How can governments improve the quality of life in cities?
questions.answer: Public transport is where I'd concentrate spending, because it addresses congestion, air quality and inequality simultaneously. Beyond that, protecting and creating green space has a disproportionate effect on wellbeing for the money involved. Housing policy matters enormously too — if ordinary workers can't afford to live near their jobs, everything else unravels. And a great deal comes down to enforcing rules that already exist.

vocab.meaning: an unusually large effect for the input kutilganidan katta ta'sir unravel fall apart gradually

practice.question: Why do young people move to big cities?
practice.answer: Mainly for opportunity. Cities have a concentration of universities, employers and cultural life. Some young people also value the anonymity — nobody is watching you or reporting back to your parents.

practice.question: Can living in a big city be lonely?
practice.answer: It can. You're surrounded by millions of people, yet city life can be curiously isolating. Long hours spent commuting leave little time for friends, and many people don't even know their neighbours' names.

practice.question: Should cars be banned from city centres?
practice.answer: Not entirely, but reducing car dependence makes sense. Several cities have closed central streets to reclaim space for pedestrians, which also cuts congestion. For older or disabled people, though, a total ban may be more trouble than it's worth.

questions.question: Why do many people enjoy water sports?
questions.answer: Part of it is simply that water makes movement feel different — you're weightless in a way you never are on land, which people find genuinely exhilarating. There's also the element of challenge, since water is unpredictable and you can't fully control it. And for a lot of people it's the setting as much as the sport; being out on open water is restorative in itself.

vocab.meaning: feeling as if you have no weight

questions.question: What kinds of water sports are common in your country?
questions.answer: Fairly limited, honestly, because we're landlocked and much of the country is arid. Swimming is the main one, though usually in pools rather than open water. There's some activity on the reservoirs — Charvak in particular attracts jet skis and small boats in summer. Rafting exists on the mountain rivers but it remains very much a niche pursuit rather than anything mainstream.

vocab.meaning: with no access to the sea
an activity followed by few people

questions.question: Do you think water sports are dangerous?
questions.answer: More dangerous than their land equivalents, yes, simply because the margin for error is smaller — if something goes wrong you may be unable to breathe, which isn't true of football. That said, the risk is heavily concentrated among people without training or supervision. Properly taught and with the right equipment, most are reasonably safe. The danger comes from overestimating your own ability.

vocab.meaning: how much can go wrong before it is serious
someone watching and guiding you nazorat, kuzatuv reasonably safe safe enough in normal circumstances
think something is greater than it is

questions.question: What are the advantages of water transportation?
questions.answer: Cost and capacity, principally — a single container ship carries what would require thousands of lorries, which makes it by far the cheapest way to move bulk goods over distance. It's also considerably less polluting per tonne carried than road or air freight. And it requires almost no infrastructure between ports, unlike railways, which have to be built and maintained the entire way.

questions.question: What are the disadvantages of water transportation?
questions.answer: Speed is the obvious one — sea freight takes weeks where air takes a day, which rules it out for anything perishable or urgent. It's also at the mercy of weather in a way other transport isn't. Environmentally, shipping fuel is genuinely dirty, and there's the constant risk of spills. And of course it only works between coasts, so you still need road transport at either end.

vocab.meaning: an accidental release of oil or chemicals

practice.question: Should all children learn to swim at school?
practice.answer: Definitely. Even in a landlocked country like ours, people swim in rivers and reservoirs every summer, and accidents happen. Lessons with proper supervision are by far the safest way to learn.

practice.question: Why do some people enjoy extreme sports?
practice.answer: Because they're exhilarating. When the margin for error is tiny, you have to focus completely, which is strangely restorative — you forget everything else. It's still a niche pursuit, though, because of the cost and the risk.

practice.question: Will water transport become more important in the future?
practice.answer: For freight, probably. Ships carry bulk goods far more cheaply than planes or lorries. But shipping is at the mercy of the weather and a handful of canals, as recent blockages showed, so it can't replace other options.

questions.question: Is it easy for adults to learn a new language?
questions.answer: Not easy, but far more achievable than the common belief suggests. Adults are actually faster at grammar and vocabulary because they can draw on concepts they already understand. Where they genuinely struggle is pronunciation and, more importantly, time — a child has hours a day of immersion while an adult has forty minutes if they're lucky. So the obstacle is circumstance rather than capacity.

questions.question: Why do some people learn languages faster than others?
questions.answer: Exposure explains most of the variation — people who read, listen and speak daily progress at a completely different rate, and that's usually mistaken for talent. Motivation matters enormously too: somebody who needs the language for work will outpace somebody studying it out of vague interest. Prior languages help, since each additional one is easier. And a willingness to sound foolish is genuinely underrated.

vocab.meaning: seem silly when you make mistakes

questions.question: What problems do language learners usually face?
questions.answer: The commonest is plateauing — rapid early progress followed by months where nothing seems to improve, which is where most people give up. Speaking anxiety is another major one; a great many learners understand far more than they can produce because they're afraid of errors. And there's the practical difficulty of finding anyone to practise with, particularly for languages not spoken locally.

vocab.uz: bir joyda to'xtab qolmoq, o'sish to'xtashi

vocab.meaning: more than you can produce have better passive than active knowledge
in the area where you live

questions.question: Should children start learning a foreign language at a very young age?
questions.answer: On balance yes, mainly for pronunciation, which is the one area where the early advantage is well established. But I'd add two caveats. It only works with genuine, regular exposure — an hour a week achieves very little and can put children off entirely. And it shouldn't come at the expense of the first language, since literacy in your own tongue underpins everything else.

vocab.meaning: someone off something make them lose interest in it

questions.question: What makes a good language teacher?
questions.answer: The ability to keep students talking, above all — the best teachers speak far less than their students do, which is the opposite of what most people assume. Knowing how to correct without discouraging is the second skill, and it's genuinely difficult. Beyond that, good teachers choose material students actually care about, because interest does more for retention than any technique.

vocab.meaning: point out and fix their mistakes

practice.question: Is it better to learn a language in class or by living abroad?
practice.answer: Immersion is hard to beat, because constant exposure forces you to use the language. Classes give you structure, though, and adults who combine both usually outpace those who rely on just one.

practice.question: Why do many learners stop making progress after a while?
practice.answer: Learners often plateau at intermediate level because they can already communicate, so the pressure disappears. Many also avoid difficult structures because they're afraid to sound foolish. Breaking through takes deliberate practice.

practice.question: Should teachers correct every mistake students make?
practice.answer: No — it can put learners off speaking entirely. Teachers should correct students on patterns that affect meaning and let minor slips go. Focused feedback also improves retention, because learners remember a few key points better than a long list.

questions.question: Is there any environmental problem in your country?
questions.answer: Several, though the most severe by far is the desiccation of the Aral Sea, which is widely described as one of the worst environmental disasters of the last century.
